#8325. 21. The Wall

They say the journey of 1000 miles starts with a single step, but what about the final step?

I felt myself slowing down as I walked over the broken earth. Once I get there, I’m there, and the hike is over.

Would the journey end at the official terminus? The escalation of border conditions had left us all uncertain. First it had been the National Defense Area visitor pass, applied for weeks ago and received. We would be checked in and allowed to reach the spike of rock that marked the end of the trail.

Then the word had come – no access at all. The terminus had been walled off on the US side. The great plan was, they said, to build a double wall to trap any would-be border crossers between them. The thirty-foot rim of steel that ran from one horizon to another wasn’t cutting it, apparently. A second one would surely do the trick, never mind that anyone can see straight through the fence, and never mind that any ladder or rope or anything of that nature could easily be passed between the bars.

Never mind that jaguar and oryx and all sorts of wild, rare and beautiful creatures need freedom of movement through the region in order to survive. People aren’t the only things that live on the land. The species of animals that have lived here since before recorded history do not live in “Mexico” or “The United States.” They simply live on the land. Only people have use for nations or walls.

With the uncertainty of our ending place, two talented hikers had built a replica of the terminus out of cardboard, and had been carrying it for over 100 miles. This was to be placed against the border wall at whatever location we were able to get to, to be our terminus if we couldn’t reach the official one.

Then the word had come from some hikers just a couple days ahead: the terminus could be accessed by walking around to a cattle guard at the side of the construction site. Neither border patrol nor the military was anywhere to be seen, and the men of the construction teams were easygoing and sympathetic to our cause. Maybe we could get through, maybe we could get there. Maybe we could finish at the terminus.

It was with these hopes and somewhat muted expectations that I walked over the last hill of rocky ground, and saw the wall for the first time, ten miles away. Dust clouds from construction. A small farming community of the far side. A black line that cut the visible world in half.

I reached the cattle guard where other hikers waited. A security man said we could go in as soon as the digger had moved on far enough down the line. More hikers arrived and waited. We sat and ate snacks and threw pebbles and looked up at the massive beams of the wall. The two parallel lines of fencing creating an optical illusion, gaps and solids that blurred with movement to disorienting effect. Any sound that was loud enough – the clapping of hands, for example – ricochetted off the angle of the beams with a sound like a laser gun in a movie. We had a little fun making the “beeowmmmm” sounds shoot down the border wall.

Then it happened. A garbled voice on the radio, somebody gave a thumbs up, and we were in. All the chatter of our wait was gone now. We marched with an inward silence for the last hundred yards of dirt to the end. The end.

The stone was warm from the sun. We spent a long time taking it in, and taking photos. There we were. It was neither good nor bad, it simply was. The obelisk, the end of the journey. There it was.

Some in our group were finishing their triple crown, and although we all were excited by our achievement, they earned a special place among us. The group of them stepped up to the monument for a group picture, and the rest of us moved away. I stepped to the older wall, the one that stood on the actual border. A cool wind moved in between the bars from Mexico. The truth is, if there had been a gate there I would’ve passed through and kept on walking. But there was no gate. There was only the wall.

A few weeks ago the trail led me past the front gate of a prison. There were inmates in the yard walking laps as I walked past. I remember being surprised at how taken aback I was – I have seen prisons and prisoners before, yet this felt hard to witness. People fenced in, walking in circles while I walked free.

I don’t know that I’ve ever been called an optimist, or a pessimist. An idealist, sure, certainly. It is not for me to say that people in prison shouldn’t be there. It is not for me to say that the border between two nations shouldn’t be protected.

Using the methods of man’s mind to separate and divide people just feels wrong. No matter how right it may be, locking people up is wrong.

Freedom of movement is the entire basis of thru hiking. Taking someone’s freedom to move is taking freedom itself. “The Trail Unites Us” was carved into one side of the monument that stood between two walls. Literally set in stone, and literally overshadowed by the powers that be.

When the time came to leave, we did so with slight bewilderment. Now what? Even though we all knew what came next in our lives, or at least had an idea, the feeling of purpose that comes with a thruhike was just…gone. There was relief at the success, excitement for the future and peace from the accomplishment, but the hike was over, and the purpose had gone with it.

We loaded up into the vehicles. Some family members had come to aid their loved ones – and the rest of us – in the finale. I climbed into the bed of a pickup with a number of backpacks. There was room for me to sit in one of the cars, but I wasn’t ready for that. I wanted to stay outside, and I was happy to have a moment alone.

Today I am thirty years old. I’ve made it this far – through my life and through the journey south. One is ending, and the other continues for however long it may. I am ready for what comes next. In the near future there will be time with friends and family, the chaos of cities, buying a car and moving into a new apartment and going back to work and all sorts of events of “regular life.” In the further future, there will certainly be another thruhike. For as long as I can, for as long as it is up to me, I will live free. For now, I sit in the solitude and peace of the windy truck bed and watch the evening lightning crackle and blaze over Mexico.

Until next time, dear readers. Live free.

#8324. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Bussom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin said. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Busson explained.

Bru Busson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Busson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”

Busson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the big cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Busson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Busson/Sanmartin

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Busson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they said. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#8321. “We Used FFS and Were Targeting Big Bass.” Angler Breaks 76-Year-Old Smallmouth Bass Record

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:14 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

On the morning of October 30 Austin Schiefer and his fishing buddy Ted Johnson launched their bass boat into Green Bay, a huge Wisconsin portion of Lake Michigan. They started about 7:30 working a reef area in 18 feet of water about two miles from shore. Before long, they’d go on to break a 76-year-old fishing record.

“It was a spot we’d fished previously and caught nice smallmouths on,” Schiefer tells Outdoor Life. “We used forward-facing sonar and were targeting big bass.”

The morning started windy, ideal conditions for clear water bass on Green Bay. The duo was catching bass, but about mid-day the wind died and the water got calm.

“That’s not the best conditions for Green Bay,” says Schiefer, who works for UPS when he’s not producing his own line of soft plastic lures (Schief’s Custom Baits). “There were plenty of bass on the reef, but they were finicky and wouldn’t take the lures I was casting.”

Johnson, however, was catching bass using a different type of soft plastic. He suggested to Schiefer that he try one of the lures he was doing well with, and to go lighter with his tackle.

“The bite was light and deep, so I changed to the setup that Ted suggested,” says Schiefer, from Menasha, Wisconsin.

Schiefer changed over to a Deps Sakamata Shad Soft Jerkbait, which is a 5-inch lure, and the productive hue was “champagne-pepper.”

He threaded the lure onto a 3/32nd-ounce jighead and made a long cast with the lightest 7-foot spinning rod he owns. His reel was spooled with 8-pound test Power Pro braided line with a 10-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

“I wanted to make a long cast and sort of swim the lure back as it sank, a pendulum like retrieve,” says Schiefer. “We could see fish on bottom with sonar, but they’d rise up to take lures. Except they were refusing my lures just before they’d hit – until I cast that Deps Jerkbait.”

It was about 2 p.m. and as Schiefer’s lure sank he felt a hit. But the fish didn’t fight like a smallmouth. The battle wasn’t fast and furious and there were no jumps. Just a couple minutes of it taking drag, and rugged deep pulling and rolling – so much so that Schiefer thought perhaps he’d hooked a freshwater drum.

“But as I worked it to the surface I got a look at it in that clear water about 10 feet down, and I saw that it was a huge smallmouth,” he says. “I knew it was a monster, and when I got it to the boat Ted netted it.

“I got lucky, because the hook was bent when I took the lure out of its mouth.”

Schiefer had caught big smallmouths previously, but nothing over 7 pounds, so he knew his catch was important. They put the lunker bass in their boat livewell and tried to contact Wisconsin’s Department of Natural Resources. But it was Friday afternoon before Halloween, and no one from the DNR was available.

The anglers quit fishing and trailered their boat to a grocery store where the bass was weighed at 9 pounds, 11ounces on certified scales. It measured 23.75 inches long. The smallmouth easily topped the 1950 Wisconsin record smallie weighing 9 pounds, 1 ounce. That fish was caught by Leon Stefonek in Oneida County’s Indian Lake.

To qualify as a state record bass, the DNR required the fish to be weighed and examined by state biologists. That didn’t happen until the next day, when DNR fisheries staff weighed and inspected the fish.

They discovered the bass was a male, not a female – which usually are the larger of the two fish genders. Additionally, Schiefer’s 9.70-pound smallmouth had nothing in its stomach, again unusual as most bass in autumn are feeding heavily for the coming winter.

Schiefer will have a skin mount made of his smallmouth bass record, which he says has been officially recognized by DNR as Wisconsin’s heaviest bronzeback of all time. He’s also considering having replica mounts made of the fish.

Read Next: 7 Forward Facing Sonar Tips: Settings, Mounting, and Techniques Explained

“I think a replica mount of the bass would be nice for the National Freshwater Fishing Hall of Fame in their Hayward museum, and maybe one for Bass Pro Shops, too,” he says.

“My only regret in all of this is I didn’t release the fish alive. I couldn’t with the DNR requirements for weighing and inspecting the fish for the record… I’ve had some sleepless nights because of that. I did everything in my power to keep from killing that bass.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8318. A Close Encounter with a Mama Bear & Cub on the Arizona Trail

This morning I woke up a little before 6AM and boiled water for coffee. Then I got packed up and we were walking by 6:30AM after the sun had come up. The section of trail that we were passing through this morning was a vast field filled with small white wildflowers. Off in the distance past the tall wheat grass and wildflowers was the massive snow-covered Mount Humphreys. We continued through the valley for some time, eventually making our way toward a small forest of pine trees.

There in the forest we passed by a bear box water cache stocked with gallons of water for hikers and bikers. Then we crossed over a dirt road by a trailhead before getting back into the forest. The trail continued through the thin pine forest for the next couple of hours. The trail itself was nice and soft beneath our feet thanks to the fallen pine needles. And our course was relatively flat and it made for some “easy” hiking.

The views this morning were truly breathtaking. I loved the color of the wheatgrass as the morning light began to shine down on it. Plus, the little white wildflowers that covered the trail matched perfectly with the snow covered mountain in the distance.

About an hour or so after leaving the water cache, we were hiking along a wide dirt road briefly. All of a sudden a group of about 4-5 friendly dogs ran up to greet us. Their owners were doing some hunting, or at least some scouting. The dogs were all adorable and really social. We got to give them all a good pet before continuing on. Then right as we were leaving one of the men mentioned that there was another dog not far behind them. This other dog was a golden retriever and was doing its own thing apparently.

Stopping off at our first water source of the day, a nice stocked up water cache.

Originally, when we were planning this section of trail from the South Rim of the Grand Canyon to Flagstaff, I packed a whole bunch of food and even was able to leave extra food in Gorf’s car. But when we did actually grab our food from her car I thought I had packed way too much and decided to leave a day or two of food behind. Now, on day 5 out of town, I was definitely running incredibly low on food. Even yesterday I really had to ration my snacks and Slide wound up giving me a couple of snacks. Today my rations were even lower, and every time Slide ate something he would give me a little bit. I think I started the morning with around 5 small bars or snacks. And today we have to hike around 35 miles if we want to make it to the trailhead to go into Flagstaff.

Slide walking on the trail ahead of me. The small white flowers adorning the trail combined with snow capped Mount Humphreys off in the distance made for an incredible morning.

It probably would have been much more relaxing to slow down and go into Flagstaff tomorrow morning or afternoon instead. But by this evening I’m going to be ravenous and it will be nice to get into town and be able to load up on food. Plus if we’re going to be charging up cameras and other electronics, it just makes more sense to stay in town overnight. Some of my devices charge fairly quickly, like my headlamp and GoPro. But my battery banks take hours to charge if they are completely out of juice.

In the late morning the trail brought us past a rusty metal sign stating that we had 611 miles remaining along the Arizona Trail. Apparently we’ve traveled 189 miles so far. At least as of this morning. The trail continued to weave through fields of tall wheatgrass and scarce clusters of pine trees. Today is a Saturday and typically the days of the week are meaningless out on the trail. But not a Saturday afternoon near Flagstaff! In my opinion, Flagstaff is to Arizona what Denver is to Colorado. Sometime in the late morning a couple of mountain bikers began going past us. In the end about 20 bikers wound up riding past in a few minutes’ time! I certainly wasn’t expecting that. We would wind up seeing many more over the course of the day as well.

Only 611 miles to go! At least as of this morning.

Well before the afternoon I was absolutely ravenous and starting to get hangry. I’m really not the type of person to typically be majorly bothered by hunger. These last couple of days though I’ve been pretty low on food. Now today I am starting to notice it making me a little bit more agitated. At least that’s how I was feeling by the time we were about 12 miles into the day. So Slide suggested that we sit down for a few minutes to each make something hot to eat. I might not have many snacks but I do have oatmeal and some ramen noodles.

Around 10:30AM Slide and I stopped off to eat hot brunch. I enjoyed some filling oatmeal and a hot chocolate. I was starving and this was just what I needed.

There was a nice spot just off the trail with a large log and a couple rocks. We sat there and boiled water for our late breakfast/early lunch. I had 2 packets of oatmeal and a hot chocolate. By the time we were packing up I felt way better.

Right as we got moving again another mountain hiker went by us. I was so glad that he didn’t catch us while we were cooking and more sprawled out. From there, the trail fluctuated between some pretty wide open views of grasslands with soft blue mountains in the distance, and denser pine forest with fairly frequent downed trees. The mountain bikers were not loving all of the down trees, but we didn’t mind. They were all easy enough to climb up and over. It would certainly be more of a hassle to be lifting a bike up and over a downed tree versus just climbing up and over it.

I’m not sure whether to call this area a prairie, valley, or just grasslands. But it sure is beautiful. A lot of the day was spent hiking through terrain such as this.

After our late breakfast break I had a whole lot more energy for the rest of the morning and afternoon. But by around 3PM my ravenous hunger had returned, and I really didn’t have anything to eat that sounded even remotely appetizing to me. All of my quality snacks were long gone, and more than anything I was just craving something filling. That is what is so amazing about town food. Afterwards you actually feel full! The food that I eat on the trail typically only makes me feel full for a little while. And the amount of snacks that it takes to get full is immense. As we continued along I was getting very excited to make it back to Flagstaff and have something delicious for dinner.

We didn’t investigate the “secret” trail but it was tempting.

The latter part of the day consisted of more hiking through patchy forests of pine trees, rather than wide-open grasslands. It made for very easy hiking and the time passed by quickly. We saw a few more bikers and people out on the trail, but not too many. Then around 4:30PM we came up to a trailhead parking lot with a privy and some cars. There were some nice rocks lining the gravel lot and we enjoyed a quick break there. At this point we had another 2.5 hours of hiking to go, which didn’t seem too bad. And we were just shy of 30 miles into the day already.

Sitting on a nice big rock at a trailhead a couple of hours before dark.

The next section of trail that we passed through was also quite forested, but traded in its pine trees for brightly colored aspens. One particular stretch of trail was bright yellow all throughout. Even the forest floor was covered in nature’s own yellow confetti. The temperature was starting to cool down around this time as the sun began to set. The early evening is typically my favorite time of the day. I love a good sunrise, but more than anything I love watching the sun set on another successful day of hiking. One of the best rewards for a long day on the trail is a perfect, cool evening.

Our previous break had been pretty short and sweet, so we wound up stopping off one last time just before 6PM. The trail passed by a couple of massive boulders just off the trail. So we decided to sit on top of one and watch the sun begin to set. We had to hike for another or so to make it to the upcoming trailhead. From there we could walk right down the road to a gas station. Then get picked up by Gorf to stay at their place for the night.

When we left our last break spot we just put our heads down and kept it moving. The surrounding area was really beautiful and traded in the pine covered trail for some deep red clay trail. Before it got dark we could see a large rock formation looming over us. Then the sun went down and we continued along to the trailhead. But before we could make it there I caught up to Slide who was stopped on the trail looking at something.

Toward the end of the day the trail changed from pine covered dirt to a red clay.

When I caught up to him he pointed at a set of eyes up in a tree which he thought were mountain lions. That was pretty exciting as I’m always eager to see some wildlife. But upon further inspection we noticed two sets of eyes, and one of them was moving down around the base of a tree. Then eventually we could see that the animal at the base of the tree was actually a small bear cub! When it had its hands up on the tree trunk it was pretty undeniable. The momma bear was actually way up in the tree above, squished onto a narrow branch.

Instead of continuing down the trail we got off and walked a little ways away to put distance between us and the bears. At this angle we could see the mom very clearly and she looked so massive up on that tiny tree branch. Then we got out of there and within a handful of minutes we were out at the trailhead. The two of us walked down the road to the gas station and Gorf pulled in just as we got there. Slide and I grabbed some goodies from the gas station and then got in the car to head back to Gorf and Slash’s place. And on our way we picked up pizza for everybody too.

Passing through a tunnel right before the trailhead into Flagstaff.

It was such a nice feeling to be back at the house again. On a thru hike it is so uncommon that you go to the same place more than once, so this is a lovely treat. It was so nice to see Gorf again and get settled into their cozy and adorable home. Slide and I showered, started laundry, and devoured a ton of Hawaiin pizza and pepperoni pizza. Then I got some other chores done such as plugging in my electronics, uploading photos and videos, and cleaning my TOAKS pot and spoon.

By now it was quite late but the night wasn’t over yet. Two other hikers, Woods and Strix, that we know are also staying here at Gorf and Slash’s place tonight! They actually got here first and had everything planned since we originally thought we might arrive tomorrow. So tonight they’re in the guest room and we made a cozy nest on the floor of the spare “yoga room” across the hall. It was perfect. At this point I was exhausted but definitely wanted to get a little bit of editing work done. I made myself stay up for another hour or so before eventually doing my stretching routine and calling it a night. Tomorrow we will have to do our resupply in the morning and then hopefully get back to trail at a fairly reasonable time.

I’m a 29 year old thru hiker who has walked over 22,000 miles over the past handful of years. In 2017 I attempted my first thru hike ever, out on the PCT. I completed 1,300~ miles in between semesters of college. Then went back in 2022 and hiked the entire trail over again. The following year in 2023 I hiked the entire 5,600 mile eastern continental trail. Which stretches from Key West, Florida all the way to Newfoundland, Canada. When I completed that trek, I became the 2nd woman in history to hike the entire trail. In 2024 I completed my thru hiking triple crown, after completing the CDT. Then in 2025 I became the 1st woman in history to complete the "border to border" calendar year triple crown. When I finished, I decided to continue hiking for the rest of the year, completing 10,070~ miles in 2025. #8317. Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#8316. These Are the 13 Tactics Expert Whitetail Hunters Actually Use to Tag Mature Bucks

Published Nov 4, 2026 5:13 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The best deer hunters in the nation (known and unknown) all share a common thread. They are students of deer and the woods, and they never stop learning. As such, they continually experiment with new and advanced deer hunting tactics.

In order to learn some of these secrets (and to share them with you), I called a handful of the best deer hunters I know. Here’s how they find success season after season.

Mark Drury of Drury Outdoors has bagged more big deer than most. His approach is proven, and the process he uses includes saving and analyzing a lot of trail camera data, especially historical information. He has kept every single trail cam pic of a racked buck since 2007.

“Save trail monitoring pictures in an organized fashion for easy review in future years,” Drury says. “Bucks are incredibly habitual from year to year. Study your pics year-round to formulate patterns with individual bucks or areas. [Over time you’ll build] a database that helps lead to patterns in future years, as crop rotations, weather, and moon in future seasons mirror conditions that occurred in the past. It takes a lot of time to assemble and study but saves time in future seasons.”

Grant Woods of Growing Deer TV is one of the most renowned deer scientists in the country. He seems to get inside the mind of whitetails and understands what they do and why they do it. To that point, he stresses making hunting decisions based on what deer do, and not what we think they should do.

“An issue I’ve seen is hunters making setup and tactical decisions based on human thoughts,” Woods says. “The hunters I know that have repeated success filling tags in all types of conditions and habitats always think like a deer. They consider what deer need that day, and what will deer avoid.”

As Paul Beasley, co-host of “Canada in the Rough” TV, says, hunters are creatures of habit. “The longer we hunt a piece of ground, the more established our hunting setups and entry/access/travel points become,” he says. “We tend to rely more on what has worked before, and while deer in general also tend to gravitate to the same trails, food sources, and pinch points, it has been my experience that mature bucks need to be treated as individuals and hunted accordingly.

“The buck I shot this year helps illustrate my point. We have hunted this same 100-acre property for over 10 years, and have always taken deer off of it in the same 50-yard-by-80-yard area. Throughout the spring and into summer, this buck was working that area perfectly, but as hunting season approached, his behavior changed. His appearances on camera began to fall off. So, I scrambled to put up more cameras and found that he hadn’t gone anywhere. He was just using different parts of the property.”

Beasley killed that buck on the second afternoon of the season. He arrowed from a setup that his crew had never harvested a buck from before.

“It was through paying attention to this individual buck’s behavior, and not just doing the same old thing that has always worked, that allowed me to put my tag on him,” Beasley says.

Oftentimes deer hunters do things without thinking. We react, rather than making decisions based on logic. HeadHunters TV’s Nate Hosie agrees, and says we should hunt smarter and not harder.

“Growing up, I used to think the more I was out there the better my chances,” he says. “It’s not completely wrong, but as I’ve grown as a hunter, I’ve learned to pick my moments for when to strike. Wind, temperature, time of year, trail cam intel, [and more] now go into my hunt. The less I’m in and out, and the higher probability my attempts are, the more success I find.”

Rick White is a longtime staple in the outdoor industry and he suggests that hunters go all or nothing with scent management.

“One of the biggest things I try to instill in people is always going to the woods as scent-free as possible,” he says. “Always play the wind. Never intentionally hunt a stand on a bad wind. But also know that deer don’t always come in from where we want them to. So, if you’re not going to follow every step with scent elimination, then save your money.”

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work

It sounds like rudimentary advice, but even experienced hunters make blunders that lead to being seen, heard, and smelled by deer. It’s something we must continually keep at the forefront of our mind. Will this entry route cause bedded deer to see me? Will this exit route blow scent into a bedding area?

Bone Collector Co-Host Nick Mundt knows deer hunting as well as anyone. As a former deer hunting guide and current big deer killer, he stresses the importance of going undetected when getting in and out of your hunting spots.

“Never think the wind will just work,” he says. “Always know that they’ll bust you if the wind is wrong. It dictates every sit.”

Aaron Gaines of Ani-Logics advises hunters to kill a target buck as early as possible. The early season and pre-rut offer opportunities to hunt consistent bucks.

“This is when he’s on a pattern and most predictable,” Gaines says. “To do this, I utilize most recent information from cameras. I’m very disciplined on hunting the right wind. If he’s daylighting, and I’ve got the right wind, things usually work out well.”

Read Next: Why the Last Week of October Is the Best Time to Kill a Big Buck

During the rut, whitetail bucks seem to travel via loops. That’s not hearsay or some hokey hack from your grandaddy’s hunting journal. That’s straight from a deer biologist. More specifically, former CEO of the Quality Deer Management Association and current HuntStand biologist, Brian Murphy.

“The biggest piece of advice I’ve learned over the years is to develop a plan and then stick with it long enough for it to have a reasonable chance of success,” Murphy says. “In other words, informed optimism. The hunters who have done their homework and keep a positive attitude, often after multiple dismal outings, are ultimately the most successful. Knowing from research that bucks often take a few days to complete loops within their home range, it’s not surprising that it takes persistence to increase the odds you will get an opportunity.”

Nathan Mrnak, COO of Base Camp Leasing, is a diehard deer hunter. He spends many days in the field each year. He stresses that it’s OK to move off your original plan and make a move.

“Picking out a stand location can be one of the toughest decisions while setting up on a mature whitetail,” he says. “I have had many first sits that ended with my target buck just out of bow range. Seeing his exact route provided the last bit of intel to moving a set just 50 yards to capitalize the next sit. This has worked time and time again in big timber.”

The most basic element of deer hunting is hunting deer where they are. To do that, you need current information.

Own the Season’s Art Helin knows this well. “Hunt where the bucks want to be during the correct phase of the season,” he says. “Food sources during early season, transition areas during the pre-rut (between field and bedding and staging areas), funnels and ridge edges during the rut (all day or mid-day sits especially), and back to food sources late season.”

During the rut, a lot of deer hunters choose to do all-day sits. Whitetail Properties Land Specialist Ben Harshyne does, too. However, he changes things up.

“I grew up hunting all-day sits in one stand,” he says. “Over time, I learned that deep timber and thick cover are action-packed in the morning and afternoon, yet often go cold by evening. In the afternoon, shift focus to hunting cover and edges near food sources or along travel lines leading to food. Not necessarily the actual food edge, but nearby. Does bed near food and still want to feed — and the bucks know it. Few stands are productive all day, so fine-tune your late-day move to target cover that relates to food.”

Big buck killer Jared Mills has arrowed a lot of big whitetails. He says don’t be afraid to be aggressive, but do it at the right time.

“I think most guys tend to be too conservative when hunting a target buck, staying on the fringes and only getting out when the conditions are perfect,” he says. “That’s fine if you have the entire season to hunt, and there’s little chance of him getting killed by a neighbor, but that’s a very rare scenario for most of us. While the windows of opportunity to encounter a target buck are already small enough, we make them even smaller by not getting in there after him. Be smart with your hunting, of course, but don’t sit around waiting for the absolute perfect time to move in, otherwise, you’ll likely miss a chance.”

Finally, just keep hunting. You won’t always kill a deer on opening day. It might just be closing day. So, keep hunting, and don’t give up.

“Have patience and persistence,” Helin concluded. “The entire season can change, and it can all happen in a short minute. Stay with it, and never give up, but also never get lazy. Always follow the same regimen from day No. 1 until the end.”

By Alex Robinson, Bob Humphrey, Tony Hansen, Craig Dougherty

#8313. The Old-School Guide to Not Getting Lost in the Woods (Before We Had GPS)

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The ridge I was on sloped gently down to a flat gap that spilled off into wide coves on either side. Through the spring and summer the forest in this mountain backcountry had been blessed with abundant rainfall and the wild creatures were busy reaping the berries, seeds and other browse. Deer tracks were everywhere and several trails crossed in the gap where deer had traveled along the ridge or moved between the high coves.

The ridge trail I followed was wet from recent rains and I pussy-footed almost without sound toward the top of a contour from which the slope pitched abruptly into the gap. I was following the general rule for a stalking deer hunter, which specifies that you walk for two counts, then pause, look and listen for four. I was in the second phase of this procedure when something moved just below me in the edge of the gap.

At first I thought I saw the haunches of a deer with its posterior toward me. But a closer look revealed a man, dressed in camouflage, on his hands and knees as though he were after doodlebugs. I moved cautiously toward him, keeping a tree trunk handy so that I could step behind it should the hunter suddenly detect or sense my presence and whirl on me with his gun, which leaned against a tree close beside him.

He was so engrossed that he did not see or hear me. I stopped a few yards away, scarcely believing my eyes. Spread out on the ground was a 6×6-foot map, with a compass propped up in its middle. He was intently studying one and then the other.

I cleared my throat. He gave a little start, straightened up and looked around.

“Oh, no,” he said and stood up. “I just wanted to see where I was going, to make sure I didn’t get lost.”

We exchanged introductions. His large-caliber rifle told me he was after big game—in this case a whitetail deer because it was the largest game animal around. I was curious about the map and compass and the way he was using them, yet I didn’t want to appear too nosey.

“Looks like you have your hunt pretty well organized,” I suggested mildly.

“Oh yes,” he said. “Then I always know where I am.”

“I’m interested,” I said. “If you don’t mind, please tell me how you do it.”

“Of course I don’t mind,” he said and smiled. “It might help you some time.”

He went back to his knees and I squatted beside him. He put his finger on a spot where he had made an X.

“Here is where I left my car,” he told me. “I took a bearing on this gap and followed a compass course to it. Didn’t miss it by more than a couple hundred yards.”

The map showed that the straight line he had followed between the two points crossed a deep cove, with steep sides. A much easier route would have been at a slight angle to his direct line, up a gentle slope to the ridge and then an almost level walk into the gap. I did not want to confuse him by pointing this out.

With his finger he traced another scope of country, then another, in a sort of rough triangle that would put him back in the vicinity of his car.

“You’ve probably seen plenty of deer sign,” I suggested, “tracks, scrapes, rubs and such.”

“Well, really I haven’t,” he admitted. “I was told this country is full of whitetails and I’m looking for a big buck.”

He stood up, folded his map, slid the rifle sling over his shoulder and looked at his compass.

“Good luck,” I said. “I hope you find him somewhere on your course.”

During many years of walking trails I have run into a number of hunters who concentrated so hard on map and compass reading that they forgot to hunt. This may be because there are many new hunters who either lack wilderness smarts or who have read articles in the magazines explaining how a man in the woods can find his way by taking bearings with a compass on top of a map. I’ve read a few of those articles and somehow got the impression that most of them were written by men who knew more about maps and compasses than they did about hunting. A man walking through the woods with a map in one hand and a compass in the other can’t devote much time to his reason for being there.

I’m not saying that a map and compass are not necessary. Both are. My old Western hunting buddy Jim Gay used to say that when a man needs a compass, it’s too late. I must disagree.

Months before I hunt any territory new to me, I write for maps. They are available from the U. S. Forest Service and a number of other federal agencies and from the states and provinces. Some maps show the trails and streams, others are contoured to indicate topography.

Everything is bordered by something. In the broadest sense of the term, North America lies generally between three oceans, the Gulf of Mexico and Canada.

Narrow this down to any segment of our vast land and you have rivers, creeks, swamps, ridges, roads and trails that surround your hunting territory, however large or small it might be. Fix those landmarks in your mind, with compass directions, and you can always come out on a road or trail that eventually leads you to where people are.

I was in Wyoming’s Thorofare wilderness with a hunter who had seen very little backcountry. One afternoon when we were moving our camp from one segment of this range to another, my friend somehow got ahead of the packstring and took the wrong trail. When night came he was very much lost. He was smart enough to stop and build a fire. In the morning he remembered what I’d told him: “Most of the Thorofare trails parallel streams, so if you get lost, go downhill until you find a creek and follow it. Eventually it will lead to a trail.”

We went looking for him after breakfast. We found where he’d branched off the main trail and we followed the tracks of his horse. They led to the remains of his fire and where he’d turned downhill to a creek that he followed to the main trail. Because we were tracking him and moving more slowly, he arrived in camp hours before we did.

Even though I think I know all the features, I normally carry a map in my backpack or saddle bags. And a number of times I have used it to help me choose the right ridge or valley.

A paper map with no backing for substance soon wears out from folding and unfolding or from hauling it around. Its life may be prolonged if you will glue it to some fabric such as sailcloth, very lightweight canvas or thin plastic. A coat of shellac helps keep it dry. Many outdoorsmen carry this type of reinforced map.

So before you hunt anywhere, get the lay of the land in mind, even if it’s only from a crudely drawn map done by someone who is familiar with the territory. It may save you from getting turned around.

I am convinced that a compass is a necessity. I often make the statement that I don’t go into the backyard at night for firewood without my compass. This may be a bit exaggerated but you can wager your last scrap of magnet that on any hunting trip I always have a compass with me. Over many years I’ve been turned around in the woods innumerable times. I’m sure that on a few of those occasions a compass kept me from getting hopelessly lost.

Once in Montana I followed a divide between two watersheds that cradled vast river systems. In the heavy timber, the crest of the divide made an awkward turn that I did not notice. When I reached this same place on my way back to camp, I discovered a ridge that branched off the one I followed. Thinking it was only a spur, I continued on. I knew something was wrong when I ran into a jumble of ridges, none of which bore any resemblance to the main divide.

I looked at my compass but it pointed in the wrong direction. I had no map with me, so I sat down, brushed away the leaves and pine needles and with a stick drew a crude map on the bare earth. I spent half an hour trying to correlate my map in the dirt, the compass, and the lay of the ridges. One of the toughest “lost” decisions I ever made was to backtrack myself to the “spur” ridge and follow that one.

An experienced woodsman subconsciously keeps track of himself by the sun, the direction of the wind and the features of the land. It’s only in a snowstorm, dense fog or on a cloudy night that he needs a compass and doesn’t hesitate to use it. A man new to wild country is not likely to think of these natural guides and sometimes not even his compass if he carries one. He makes a common and often serious mistake, when he is not on a trail or road, of trying to go out of the woods the way he came in. Without knowing it, he begins to walk in circles.

I have helped find a few lost hunters who stumbled for a day or two—or more—around in a circle. One was within a few hundred yards of a broad highway. If he had stopped long enough to listen, he would have heard the noise of cars passing. We found another staggering a few steps and falling, then getting up to stagger a few more steps. He had thrown away his gun, his clothes were torn and his face looked like he’d just come out of the heavyweight championship ring. He didn’t even recognize his friends.

Only two of the men we found had accepted the fact that they were lost and calmly built a fire to wait it out. One had responded to calls from the search party. The other, after a day and a night, had resorted to the universal signal of danger or distress known to almost every hunter. He fired three quick shots, waited a few minutes then fired three more. After a couple of hours he went through the same procedure and this time was heard by one of his companions.

If any man is blessed with a sense of direction, I have yet to meet him. Animals are said to have the homing instinct, but I have encountered circumstances that cause me to doubt that in unknown country they do either. Once in the northern Yukon Territory, two weeks by packstring travel from man-made trails, we hunted all day away from camp. Late in the afternoon we stalked a big bull caribou and, by the time we had made our kill, caped out the scalp and quartered and loaded the meat on our packhorse, the night was pitch black. I suggested we broil a slab of the meat and make it back to camp the next morning.

“Don’t worry about it,” the guide assured me. “These horses can go straight to camp.”

They went to camp that night but they didn’t go straight. By scent they backtracked themselves over the entire route we had taken that day, climbing ridges, following streams and hollows over the same circuitous route we had hunted. We passed areas I recognized, even in the darkness, and got back to camp only an hour or two before daylight.

Back to man’s sense of direction: Put the best woodsman you know in an insulated room, sketch a tailless donkey on the wall and give him the tail to pin in place. Blindfold him, turn out the lights, walk him in a few circles, spin him around a time or two, then noiselessly leave him in the completely dark sound-proof room to complete his mission. The odds are four to one that he won’t find the right wall and 50 to one that he won’t go directly to the derriere of the donkey.

To test your own sense of direction, leave the boat dock on a large lake where you know every shoreline and try to cross the lake in a dense fog to a spot you think you can reach with your eyes closed. Without a compass you may end up on any shore of the lake, even the one you pulled away from.

I had this experience on a wide saltwater estuary called Buttermilk Sound on the Georgia coast. We had no compass on the boat. The fog moved in, the tide was at flood and the water surface as smooth as the top of a billiard table. We thought we knew these waters well enough to ease across at slow speed but, when we began to bounce over our own wake, I suggested we drop anchor right where we were.

With the motor off we could hear a faint roar that one of our crew members identified as surf on the outer beaches and that another said was the roar of highway traffic on the mainland in the opposite direction. If we guessed wrong or continued to move in circles on an outgoing tide and if the fog persisted for a day as it sometimes did, we could have ended up on the Atlantic Ocean—out of sight of land and without a compass. We sat anchored in Buttermilk Sound for eight hours until the fog lifted. Never since have I been in a boat without a compass in my pocket or tackle box.

In the woods, even with a compass, when I have had my mind on trailing or locating game, I’ve been so badly turned around that I was inclined to dispute the compass needle. This is more likely to happen in a swamp or other flatland where every tree or clump of brush looks like every other tree or clump of brush. I have been so dead sure of my directions that I think the compass needle has gone haywire or that I’m reading the wrong end. If you’ve had that experience, you know how agonizing it is to go with the needle and against your better judgment.

Once I allowed a swamper to talk me out of using either my compass or my judgment. We had hunted until almost dark in the swamp on the Georgia side of the Savannah River between Georgia and South Carolina. We came to a trail through the swamp and I consulted my compass.

“This should lead us to high land,” I said, pointing.

“No,” he replied, indicating the opposite direction. “This is the way back to the road.”

I showed him the compass and tried to explain but he was stubborn. “I’ve lived in this swamp most of my life,” he said, “I know the way out.”

So I yielded and went with him. Half an hour later we came to the Savannah River. He stared at the rolling waters with a look of disbelief. Even then he did not concede his faulty sense of direction. “My God,” he said. “We’re in South Carolina.”

Read Next: The 11 Most Common Survival Mistakes That Will Get You Killed in the Backcountry

I watch my compass often, even when I’m in woods I know. It’s so easy to climb a ridge or go through a hollow with a different angle from the way you are traveling. And such sudden shifts of contour may turn you around.

We were 200 miles west of Anchorage, Alaska, in the expansive delta country of the Lower Kuskokwim River. The land is made up of lakes, marshes, low hills and running streams and you can get mixed up without too much effort. The guide and I had been traveling since dawn in a circle from our camp on Hewlitt Lake. I’d been watching the compass all day and late in the afternoon we waded a small stream and stood at the base of a low ridge.

“It’s getting late,” he said. “We’d better go to camp.”

I agreed and he led off in what I considered the wrong direction.

“Wait a minute,” I called. “Camp is over that way.”

“No, it’s not,” he declared emphatically. “This is the way we go.”

I showed him the compass. “I’ve been watching this all day,” I said.

“The heck with them things,” he said. “I don’t believe in all that foolishness.”

“OK, partner,” I said. “You take any direction you want. I’m going to camp.”

He hesitated a minute and then grumbled. “All right. I’ll go along. A guide is supposed to stay with his dude, no matter how crazy the guy is.”

We climbed the low hill, fought our way through a half-mile thicket of devil’s club and came out on the lake shore 100 yards above camp.

“That son of a gun was lucky to have me along,” I overheard my guide confide to the cook a little later. “Without me, him and his compass never would have found the way back here.”

If you think a map or compass is for tenderfeet or cheechakos, try being lost for a few days in the backcountry and you might change your mind.

#8310. Just as the Rut Kicks Off, 2 Popular Climbing Stick Companies Issued Recalls

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:55 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Two hunting equipment manufacturers, Latitude Outdoors and Hunt Arsenal, have issued immediate stop-use notices following reports of potentially dangerous equipment failures. Both companies are investigating the reported issues and advising customers to discontinue use until further notice. Here’s what you need to know.

Latitude Outdoors has issued an immediate stop-use notice for its popular Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks after receiving reports of steps moving, slipping, or detaching from the climbing stick posts. This system of climbing sticks was popular among public-land hunters and even won our review of the best climbing sticks (before these safety concerns came to light).

A company representative says the company identified the bottom step as the point of failure after several customer complaints.

Latitude acquired Treestyx LLC in late 2025 and subsequently introduced the Carbon Synergy Climbing Stick. The product retained the original Treestyx design and construction while incorporating a new knotless attachment method.

According to Latitude, earlier versions of the product met industry testing requirements, and the Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks underwent additional testing and recertification before their release. Warranty claims involving the step-to-post connection have raised concerns about the product’s reliability, however, ultimately resulting in its recall.

Although the company said the reported failures represent a small percentage of products in use, it is advising all customers to stop using Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks immediately.

Latitude is offering full refunds to customers, regardless of where the climbing sticks were purchased. Customers who purchased directly through Latitude can initiate a return through the company’s online portal and receive a prepaid shipping label. Refunds are also available for Carbon Synergy Illuminators and Carbon Synergy Stealth Strip Kits purchased directly from Latitude.

Customers who purchased Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks through authorized retailers should return them to the original retailer for a refund.

Retailers have also been instructed to discontinue sales and remove affected products from inventory. For more information, visit Latitude Outdoors’ return portal and see their official recall notice.

Obviously, this poses a major problem for deer hunters who are in the field now. Some social media commenters even claimed that they were going to take the risk and use the recalled sticks anyway, since they were already on their hunting trip.

Another popular saddle hunting company, Hunt Arsenal, has also issued an immediate stop-use notice for its 2026 Maxx Step Double and Triple Aiders. According to Hunt Arsenal, the attachment cord connecting the aider to the climbing stick may fray, separate or break during use, creating a serious fall hazard. The stop-use notice advises any customer using 2026 Maxx Step Double or Triple Aiders to stop using them immediately, even if the attachment cord appears undamaged.

While the company works on a solution, Hunt Arsenal advises customers to set affected products aside and not return or discard them until further instructions are provided. Hunt Arsenal expects to provide additional information early in the week of Nov. 9, including instructions for customers who purchased directly from the company or through authorized dealers. Hunters unsure whether their aider is a 2026 model should also discontinue use until they can confirm its production year.

The company said reports received so far involve only 2026 production models, and it is investigating a possible manufacturing issue that may have damaged the cord in some units. The Maxx Step Single Aider is not affected by the notice.

Updates will be available through Hunt Arsenal’s website and social media.

#8309. Slow Mornings, Friends, & Hikers in Flagstaff

This morning I was surprised how early I woke up in the room. I was up pretty late last night doing some editing. Nevertheless we were up bright and early and were both ravenously hungry for some breakfast. Once we got up we decided to just walk down the road to a nearby breakfast spot to eat. I wound up getting a chorizo eggs Benedict that had avocado and a chipotle sauce on top. Plus a pumpkin spiced chai latte, which was absolutely delicious.

Slide and I got a delicious breakfast before heading out of Flagstaff.

After we had a wonderful breakfast, we headed back to the house and met up with Gorf. Then she drove us to the grocery store to do a quick resupply. I still had some food left at the house from when we went into the Grand Canyon. But definitely needed a bit more for this next stretch of trail which is going to be 130 miles long. I did such a bad job packing out food for the last stretch and now I’m determined to get it right this time. I knew I needed more crunchy snacks like chips or goldfish. I think this time around I definitely got some more exciting things to eat. Hopefully it will be enough and I’ll also enjoy eating all the goodies I got. Resupplying is always a struggle for me because my appetite and cravings really ebb and flow on the trail. It seems like I can never get it exactly right, even after all the miles I’ve hiked in the past.

This snack made me crack up. I know it’s just a random brand of meat stick, but I think it’s hilarious that Mr. Beast makes meat sticks.

While we were getting packed up, two other hikers named Leaf and Handy came by the house. Leaf is going to hike out with Strix and Woods and be on the trail for the next couple of weeks. They wound up heading out a little bit before us and I believe Handy drove them all to the trailhead. An hour or so later we were all packed up and Gorf drove us back to the same gas station from last night. From there we could walk a short distance and be right back on the trail.

Just after noon we got dropped off back at the gas station from last night.

I packed out a couple of slices of pizza from last night which I enjoyed in the first hour or so of the day. I never liked Hawaiin pizza in my entire life until last years calendar year triple crown hike. In Damascus, Virginia I had some Hawaiin pizza and enjoyed it for the first time in my life. And now I love it! That was a great way to start off another day of hiking. Plus the trail was really flat leaving town. Apparently we can expect some generally flat and easy terrain until we get closer to Pine, AZ, our next resupply location. That’s great news because we have some major mileage standing in between us and the next town. Hopefully if we can hike around 20 miles today and then do 3 more big mile days, then we could get into town the morning that the storm is going to hit. But that will require doing about 35 miles a day for the next few days after today. That’s not a bad price to pay though in my opinion if it means avoiding most of the weather.

A cool piece of art right on the trail. This was in a section of trail with numerous short scenic loops.

Early on into our day the trail passed through an area that had some small loop trails which are popular for day hikers. We actually wound up doing a small loop by accident instead of turning off and continuing on the Arizona trail. We didn’t even realize until we had looped back to a sign that I recognized from earlier in the day. Luckily we didn’t waste too much time doing that and it was pretty funny to be honest. Plus the trail was almost entirely flat, so it wasn’t too big of an error.

Bright happy yellow flowers alongside the trail.

Sometime after that we got onto a wider double-track dirt road. This brought us past a train track and we got to watch a train go by. Not long after that it began to rain on us lightly as well, which I wasn’t expecting. With an umbrella, though, I hardly even mind a light rain! It was comfortable enough. The timing was great actually and we wound up passing through a large tunnel a little while after the rain started. We had been going for a while so it was a great opportunity to stop off for a break and stay out of the rain. Otherwise we probably would have just continued on until the rain stopped. Taking a break on trail when it’s raining is not very enjoyable and I tend to avoid it unless I’m really in dire need of a rest.

Bright, colorful graffiti at a tunnel that the trail passed right through.

The trail itself looked stunning today thanks to all of the recent weather. The wildflowers were bright and blooming and all of the green foliage was so lush. I’m assuming that Arizona doesn’t typically look like this in the fall! A lot of hikers tend to do the trail in the spring to enjoy more water on trail and more lush plant life. Getting tons of rain isn’t necessarily great for us, but it sure does make for some beautiful hiking conditions. The plants are clearly very happy about it themselves.

Slide taking some photos of the passing train.

After our tunnel break we continued going past the trail tracks and saw another train go by. Then the trail brought us through a couple more long tunnels which was really neat. One was a double tunnel too! We passed through a first long tunnel, exited briefly, and then went right back into another. I enjoyed looking at some of the nicer graffiti on the walls of the tunnel. One particular piece was of a large meerkat or groundhog-type animal. Some of the graffiti was actually pretty dang good!

I liked this cute little guy that was graffiti’d on one of the tunnels.

Around this time the rain let us and ceased for the remainder of the evening which was delightful. The trail continued to be nice and easy and we were making pretty great time. Our only hope for the day was to try to go around 20 miles. That would leave us with 3 big days of hiking in order to get to town hopefully on Thursday morning. Today is Sunday, and the storm is looking like it is going to start on Thursday and continue on through Saturday evening. I can’t believe we are even considering taking another 2 or so days off-trail for another set of storms. But I do not mess around with major rain in the desert. Flash flooding is more common than people think, plus river crossings become quite dangerous when that much water is flowing down from higher ground.

It was a gloomy, rainy day but wound up being pretty perfect! Aside from a little bit of mud on the trail.

Just before dark the trail changed a bit and began bringing us past some tall rock structures. There was a continuous rock wall on our right side for a while as we made our way down the trail, enjoying the last bit of daylight. We had already made it quite far fortunately and it was looking like we would only have the hike until just after dark. We wound up making it about 18 miles and then began searching for a place to camp for the night. The spot where we got set up even seemed like it might have some great views of the sunrise in the morning, which would be lovely.

The trail followed along this rock wall for a while which was a nice change of scenery later in the day.

It didn’t take long to find a nice flat place for the two of us to get set up. Once my tent was up and everything was inside I got comfortable and had a bit of dinner. Then did a bit of scanning through the maps on Far Out to access how far we might have to go the next couple of days. It’s looking like we’ll have to do 35 miles or more for the next two days, then hopefully the third day will be a little bit shorter. If we really push, we might be able to make it to the trailhead and road Wednesday evening. If we could get into town before the rain started that would be great. But more likely we will have a few miles to hike on Thursday morning. Then we might just have to try and hitch into town while it’s raining. That is never an easy task, but I’m hopeful. After doing a bit of planning I wound up doing my stretching and then rolling over and calling it a night.

If you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

Views of the trail just before the sun began to set. Tonight we only hiked for a little while into the dark before getting set up at camp.

#8303. Bystanders Form Human Chain To Rescue Two Hikers Who Slipped From Yosemite’s Half Dome Cables

In a daring rescue originally reported and verified by SFGATE, a group of hikers on Yosemite National Park’s Half Dome formed a human chain to rescue an engaged couple clinging to the steep slope after slipping from the cables.

On October 12, a woman descending Half Dome’s famous cable system reportedly lost her footing and began sliding away, eventually coming to rest just above a sheer drop-off.

Another hiker who was present at the time described hearing the woman’s screams just as he and his son finished descending the cables themselves. “I just was shouting, ‘No, no, no!’ because I knew she was dead,” the hiker told SFGATE. And then she stopped, and I just couldn’t believe it.”

Hikers on Half Dome’s cable path in 2025. Photo: Anna McKinney Smith

The woman’s fiancé reportedly left the cable path to help her but also slipped and ended up hanging onto a small ledge by his fingertips.

Hikers who witnessed the pair’s predicament called 911 and began assembling a makeshift chain of carabiners, slings, and doubled rope from their own supplies.

According to SFGATE, one hiker climbed down to the stranded man and helped him back to the cables while a human chain of hikers braced the line. Once safe, the man immediately joined the human chain to help reach his fianceé farther down the cliff.

The existing rope chain was too short to reach her, so the hikers extended it by linking together several climbing harnesses donated by bystanders.

Yosemite’s Half Dome. Photo via Katie Jackson

As the wind picked up and light snow began to fall, another hiker climbed down to her and helped her back to safety, aided by those bracing the line further up the slope.

The rescued couple reportedly embraced at the base of the cables and hugged the rescuers, with the fiancé weeping and promising to buy the group beers once they returned from the 16-mile round-trip trail.

Featured image: Hikers on Half Dome’s cable path in 2025. Photo: Diego Acuna
