#8302. The 10 Best Rimfire Scopes of 2026: Budget to Precision Optics Tested

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:12 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A rimfire rifle used to be the next step up from a Red Ryder. You’d grab it to plink at the range, teach a new shooter, or shoot a few squirrels. But rimfire rifles have evolved, and so has the entire hobby of shooting them. It’s now completely normal to expect a rifle to shoot 1-inch groups at 100 yards and a range session to stretch from 25 to 300 yards.

Scopes have kept pace with the rifles. You might find a basic 3-9x on a stock 10/22, but you won’t find one on someone’s RimX build. Today’s rimfire shooter wants close-focusing adjustable parallax, a first-focal-plane reticle, and plenty of elevation travel to reach well beyond 100 yards.

I selected the best rimfire scopes with those demands in mind, but I haven’t forgotten the utilitarian and budget friendly scopes. Here are my top picks from my testing and our optics tests.

I use rimfires for hunting, fun shooting and occasionally competition. I’d typically need at least two scopes to cover those pastimes: a handy 3-9x for hunting and a 3-15x for shooting small targets at extended ranges. But the Nightforce NX6 2-12×42 F1 can take on all of those uses, and do them well.

We tested the entire NX6 line at Outdoor Life’s 2026 optics test, and I was thoroughly impressed with the 5-30x56mm F1’s ability to ring steel at 300 yards and focus down to 11 yards. That scope is a bit big for my typical rimfire uses. The 3-18x is a highly versatile option that Outdoor Life Editor-in-Chief, Alex Robinson, recently picked as the best high-end scope for deer hunting, but it’s still a bit heavy for my taste. The 2-12x is my pick for the ultimate rimfire scope because it’s ideally suited for small-game hunting, plinking and shooting steel beyond 100 yards. While it’s not the scope you want for hitting tiny targets at long range, it has enough magnification to hit rimfire-sized targets around 100 yards, and I routinely shoot my KYL rimfire rack with it at 50 yards.

The scope’s attributes extend beyond its versatility. It has decent glass, an incredibly easy-to-use zero stop, close focusing and excellent tracking. Some might find the FC-MRx reticle too busy, but I like it for fast holdovers and its reference points for wind holds.

I currently have the NX6 2-12×42 on a CZ 457 American with a Proof Research carbon-fiber barrel. The rifle is a hammer and very light, and the NX6 is right at home on it.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review: Quarter-Inch Groups Right Off the Rack

If you’re looking for to compete in NRL22, there are several excellent scopes to choose from. But the Razor HD Gen III 6-36×56 is my overall best pick. It focuses down to 10 yards, has 36 MRAD of elevation adjustment, and plenty of magnification for shooting matchsticks and other tiny targets. The new VMR-5 reticle is a nice clean reticle that’s ideal for people who prefer dialing and you can still get the EBR-7 reticle if you prefer holdovers.

Here’s what optics editor, Andrew McKean, had to say about the Razor HD Gen III after our optics test:

Vortex might have been satisfied with simply upgrading the reticle inside its flagship precision scope, which has won enough PRS and NRL matches to qualify as a class leader. But with the new Gen III version of the venerable Razor HD, Vortex has created a new turret system that is precise, smart, and innovative.

The heart of the turret update is what Vortex calls its L-TEC+ zero system in which relaxing a single set screw allows users to make fast and precise turret adjustments. The system allows zeros to be established between the turrets’ .1 MRAD clicks, meaning that shooters no longer have to be satisfied with turrets set a half click above or below their true zero, a fudge factor that is more problematic the farther you shoot.

The operation takes a bit of getting used to. Tester John B. Snow, thinking the external slot on the head of the turret was designed to accept a beefy screwdriver bit, reefed on our sample, breaking the pot-metal, before reading the instructions and learning that once the retaining screw is loosened, the turret moves easily with only fingertip tension. Our other rifle-range revelation: The creepy caterpillar-looking grub that emerges from the base of the turret is not an embedded chrysalis but rather a smart revolution indicator that becomes fully emergent on the third full rotation of the elevation turret.

For the smart turret updates, the Vortex wins our Innovation Award, but that’s hardly the only update to this excellent scope. The new EBR-7D reticle is a marvel of efficient simplicity. Built around a .03 MRAD red-illuminated center dot with open aiming cross, the reticle’s elevation steps are in .2 MRAD hatches, and windage steps in .2 MRAD dots. We would like to see slightly bolder indexing, as the reticle references were hard to see below about 11-power.

The image delivered by the Razor HD is one of the best in the class, and we liked the turret indexing and smart and useful pull-to-turn illumination control. With a very close parallax adjustment and the infinitely adjustable zero, this would make an excellent rimfire competition scope.

Vortex is understandably proud of this scope, but with a retail price of around $4,000, we think it’s pretty pricey compared with its peer group. — Andrew McKean

There’s not much innovative or surprising here, just a basic duplex reticle inside a straight-ahead scope with decent turrets and a durable build. Backed by an excellent warranty.

If simplicity is the pathway to versatility, then the Vortex Crossfire II is at home on a small-game bolt rifle or a fast-shooting AR. It might not have the chops for precision work, but the duplex reticle is fast and reliable. The controls are a little mushy, but the eye relief and eye box are both forgiving and the fixed parallax makes it a great plinking scope. — Andrew McKean

Another in a long line of solid, bright Hawke scopes. This sub-$450 Vantage 30 is an upscale sibling to the Vortex Crossfire HD 6-18×50. Both sport useful second focal-plane BDC reticles with center-dot illumination. But the Hawke brings a little more sophistication to its controls, with exposed pull-to-turn turrets, immersive field of view, and a floating center-dot aiming point that lights up in either green or red.

Optics are good but not great. The illumination is good but we wish it was more intense to boost visibility in bright sunlight. And turret tracking started to slip a bit at the very end of its elevation travel.

But the Hawke impressed us with its smooth, tactile controls, and the BDC reticle is fast, with MOA-based references that correspond to the drop of standard center-fire loads. With a 50-yard zero with our standard 40-grain CCI .22 LR ammunition, we easily stretched the reticle to 300 yards by dialing 35 MOA of elevation and holding another 10 MOA. That’s impressive range for the scope-and-rimfire combo.

“It’s a simple, straightforward hunting scope that’s priced about right,” says tester Dale Manning. Enough said. — Andrew McKean

One of the surprises of the test is how testers universally fell in love with this little, versatile scope. On the surface, it seems like an oddball. Less than 10 inches long, it requires a cantilever mount to fit most rifle receivers, and it looks more like an LPVO than a serious precision scope.

But once you get behind the GPO Centuri Compact, a whole world is revealed through the excellent milling reticle. At lower magnifications with the illumination at its highest intensity, the reticle functions as a point-and-shoot red-dot sight. But at higher magnifications, starting about 10x, the reticle’s precision references become visible. A series of .1 MRAD hashes enables pinpoint aiming. For shooters who prefer to dial, the big exposed turrets pull to turn and move with authority. A smart revolution indicator pops up on the elevation turret when shooters enter the second revolution.

​If you’d rather tune the reticle to your specific load, GPO offers a free custom ballistic turret with purchase. That’s an additional value for a scope that’s already priced fairly at about $650.

Testers debated the best use cases for the Centuri Compact. Some felt it’s best suited to an AR carbine. Others wanted it on their big-woods whitetail rifle, and still others felt it would be an excellent scope for stalking elk in dark timber. That latter use is enabled with a smart illumination that lights up the floating center dot and inverted horseshoe. The red illumination is infinitely adjustable thanks to a rheostat control.

​The eyebox is stingy at higher magnifications, which forces shooters to have perfect alignment. But that’s a minor miss. The scope garnered enough pluses to finish in the top third of the field of scopes that are much more squarely configured for hunting.— Andrew McKean

The Busnell R7 won the editor’s choice award for being the best hunting scope of the year. While it’s an excellent big-game optic, it’s also right at home on a rimfire rifle. Here’s McKean’s take on this excellent piece of glass:

With this big, bright, and surprisingly sophisticated R7, Bushnell is restoring its relevance as a first-order hunting optic brand. The first focal-plane scope has an open tree-style reticle that’s anchored by an illuminated segmented circle and floating center dot that enables precision work as well as fast holdover and wind-informed shots at game.

For hunters and target shooters who would rather dial, the pull-to-turn elevation turret is nicely indexed and moves with positivity. The windage dial is capped.

Bushnell has invested heavily in the R7 line, which is the best of the Good/Better/Best product-line hierarchy that started with the R3 a couple years ago and continued with the R5 last year. The company has four different configurations of the R7, released just this month: a 1-8×24 LPVO, a 2-10×42, and a 3-15×50 in addition to the 4-20×50. The lower magnification scopes are available in second-plane reticles, but the two higher-mag versions come in either first- or second-plane reticles and either MIL or MOA, giving buyers a crazy number of variations on the platform.

We tested the second-plane MOA version of the 4-20×50, but for its versatility, performance on a wide range of targets and distances, and its flawless handling, we named the FFP R7 not only best Bushnell in the test, but the best overall hunting scope in the field of 25 excellent competitors. They include Nightforce’s new NX6, Leupold’s VX-4HD, and Zeiss’s new V3 families, along with some excellent submissions from Vortex, Trijicon, and Burris.

For its overall performance, the Bushnell R7 4-20×50 is this year’s Editor’s Choice winner as the top hunting scope of 2026.

The scope stacked points with a combination of good ED Prime glass, clear indexing on its controls, tight and positive turret and focus controls, and an illuminated Hybrid Dot Tree reticle that splits the difference between a precision competition and a hunting reticle. Its zero stop, which we’re glad to see on this type scope, is a 6-screw affair that’s a hassle to set, but works wonderfully as a solid backstop on elevation turret travel.

We worried about the durability of the R7, but it passed our inaugural drop test without skipping a beat. We dropped the scope three times from three feet on concrete covered by a 2-inch pad, and the Bushnell retained its zero.

Of course, our test teased out some deficiencies. The reticle references aren’t especially visible until about 7x, and I’d like to see one or two more intensity steps to the center-dot and segmented circle illumination to make them pop in daylight.

But if you’re looking for a rimfire or long-range competition scope that you can easily transition into a big-game hunt, this is a wonderful choice. The price, at about $950, is fair for the versatility and fine handling of this true crossover scope. — Andrew McKean

Set-it-and-forget-it hunters will appreciate this solid, honest scope for its lack of adornments. No illumination. A simple plex reticle in the second focal plane. It’s like the Fullfield mentioned above but with better glass and controls.

But hunters who are practiced at ranging a target, then dialing an aiming solution based on ballistic solvers will go crazy for this new configuration of the venerable Burris Veracity. The elevation knob is exposed, nicely indexed, and ready to dial. A little too ready, as it doesn’t lock. For some OL testers, that’s a problem, as an exposed turret can easily get pushed off zero given the hard knocks of the field.

But Burris has that figured out, too, with a zero stop that ensures a return to zero. It’s a tedious 6-screw affair to set, but once the zero stop is established, it is a rock-solid baseline for dialing.

​Given the wave of hunting scopes containing first-plane reticles with busy windage and elevation references and illumination modules, this iteration of the Veracity is refreshing. But it also forces users into either dialing for distance or sticking with the single aiming point at the crosshairs. We’d rather see the 3-15×44 Veracity with the illuminated RC-MOA (Rapid Cross) reticle that gives hunters the option of dialing or using reticle references to hold for elevation and wind.

We quibble a bit at the $1,000 price for such a stripped-down scope, but the turret tracking was among the best in the field, and Burris’s “Knob Synergy” elevation dial is tight, positive, and the low-profile build won’t hang up in the field. All in, the 3-15×44 version of the Veracity is a welcome addition to the 2.5-12×42 and 5-25×50 versions. — Andrew McKean

Combining simple controls and a modest but versatile magnification range, this durable scope is perfect for just about any .22 or .17, whether for small-game hunting, plinking, or most precision target work. It has good glass, repeatable controls, and enough holdover references on the vertical stadia that, with some practice, you can extend your range out to 100 yards and longer. At close to $300, it’s priced in the meaty middle of the market and can easily transition from a first-gun optic to just about any other rifle, whether a rimfire or not.

Here’s a rimfire scope for just about any purpose. This outwardly pedestrian optic has a lot going on between a surprisingly precise second-plane reticle, bright glass, and fun indexing on the nicely tactile turrets. The best thing you can say about any scope is that it is consistent, and the VX-Freedom delivers bullets with pleasing reliability. It’s a good rabbit and squirrel scope. Still, the MOA-based references on the vertical crosshair make it a decent option for engaging distant targets, which means you don’t have to invest in a ponderously big first-plane target scope to take titles at NRL22 competitions. Lastly, the Leupold rimfire scope brings the company’s good glass and an excellent warranty.— Andrew McKean

Tract’s 22 FIRE series has a full series of scopes for .22 and .17 shooters, but this AO model (it stands for Adjustable Objective) is the most versatile scope in the line from the direct-to-consumer brand. The duplex reticle features a fine crosshair with a .25 MOA center dot, which allows for full view of the target and precise bullet placement, which competitive bullseye target shooters will appreciate.

The adjustable objective enables precise focus for targets inside 10 yards all the way out to infinity, a feature you don’t often see on rimfire-specific scopes. The objective focus is a little clunky compared with the side parallax of most modern scopes, but it works well and further enables precise shooting. At about $275 it’s not a cheap scope, but the glass is good, the controls are some of the best in the business, and the precision it allows also makes it a killer squirrel scope. — Andrew McKean

The Burris Eliminator 6 is the easy button for long-range shooting. It ranges, calculates ballistics, and tells you where to aim. Here’s what shooting editor, John B. Snow, said about the Eliminator 6 in his precision scope buying guide:

This is the most innovative scope in this roundup. Burris has long been a category leader in scopes with integrated rangefinders, and Eliminator 6 is the newest iteration of that tech. Once the scope has been fed a ballistic profile and zeroed — neither process is overly complicated — it delivers impressive point-click-and-shoot capability.

The second focal plane reticle contains a multitude of LED illumination points. When you range your target — which is done via a large button on the left side of the scope or through a remote Bluetooth switch — one of those dots lights up indicating your hold. It is remarkably idiot-proof.

I know we live in an age of technological marvels, but the fact that you can roll through the scope’s magnification range and the aiming dot will slide up and down the crosshair continuously displaying the correct hold is remarkable.

Targets beyond 1,000 yards can become difficult to laze, and you’ll likely need to fine-tune your ballistic profile to keep the scope’s solutions spot-on. But within 800 yards this system couldn’t be quicker or easier to employ. — John B. Snow

Your first consideration if you’re in the market for a rimfire rifle scope is how well it will perform with the short-range capabilities of the caliber. You probably don’t need a ton of magnification or reticle references if all you want is to shoot tin cans or 50-meter bullseye targets. But the world of rimfire shooting is evolving to look a lot like long-distance center-fire precision shooting, with all sorts of precision rimfire competitions and games that put a premium on both short-range and long-range precision. For backyard plinkers, you probably just want a simple scope with a duplex reticle, but for the latter, you’re going to want a first-plane reticle with lots of turret adjustment. Then there are the pure small-game scopes. These are lower-magnification optics with just enough reticle references to get you on game and maybe make longer shots, head-shooting squirrels, for instance.

For small-game hunting, I want a scope that gets on target fast, has a reticle that “pops” from the background, but has enough references for me to place bullets precisely out to about 75 or 100 yards. In this collection, the standout hunting scope is Bushnell’s Trophy Quick Acquisition (QA), a 1-6×24 marvel that points quickly, has an illuminated center dot for low-light work, and enough holdover references for longer shots. Others worth a look: Vortex’s Crossfire II, and Tract’s 22 FIRE. At the other end of the spectrum is EOTECH’s expensive 1-10×24 Vudu, which doubles as a marvelous AR optic. Or consider Leupold’s VX-Freedom. Its simple duplex reticle is fast and reliable.

I like lower-power scopes for most rimfire work, whether that’s hunting or target shooting. A 2-7-power or even 1-8-power will give you all the magnification you need for most purposes. But if you’re interested in the precision rimfire competitions, then you’re going to want more magnification to really see the nuances of distant targets. For those times, I’d go with a 5-20-power or 4-16-power range, and make sure that precision target scopes also have manual focus—often called parallax—to bring targets of whatever distance into crisp focus.

The price of rimfire scopes ranges all the way from about $100 up to nearly $2,000. There are problems with both ends of that spectrum, just as there are great deals as long as you know what attributes you want and how you’ll use the scope. Starting at the lower end of the price spectrum, I’d be a little leery of super-cheap scopes, simply because they are probably made with substandard components and may not be as durable as higher-priced models. If you spend under $100 on a scope, make sure it has a good warranty that will cover any breakage or malfunctions. But you can buy a lot of scope for under $200. Scopes in this roundup include Bushnell’s Trophy QA and Vortex’s Crossfire II, and both the Leupold VX-Freedom and Tract’s 22 FIRE AO are both priced around $300 and offer excellent durability, utility, and warranties. Precision rimfire scopes can be especially expensive, largely because their precision controls and components are built to a higher standard. Still, the Sightmark Presidio, priced under $400, and the Vortex Strike Eagle are both worth looking at for budget precision options. On the other end of the spectrum, both the EOTECH Vudu and Blackhound Emerge offer tons of precision for rimfire shooters, but have all the attributes to transition once you move up to center-fire precision target shooting.

Somehow, the optics industry has squeezed all the fun out of rimfire shooting. Instead of cheap, reliable, and utilitarian rifles, we now have fancy chassis rifles with all the attributes of their big-bore brethren. And prices to match. We’ve complicated what was once the most fun and simple type of shooting into rigorous competition. That’s all great if you want to make .22 shooting into a serious thing, but don’t forget that rimfires are the gateway for most shooters and hunters into our community, and the scopes and rifles that are the best for new shooters are often the most simple and cheap. So read this review with a little bit of skepticism. There are optics for every stage in a shooter’s evolution, but maybe pay special attention to those fun, simple, gateway scopes.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8298. Best Ammo for Deer Hunting, Tested for Accuracy

Published Nov 5, 2026 1:02 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Every major ammunition company has a specific product line dedicated to whitetail hunters. Ideally, this ammo will provide good accuracy, function reliably, be widely available, and deliver consistent terminal performance – all at a wallet-friendly price.

I tested six popular whitetail loads to compare their precision at the bench, how they fed and cycled, and the consistency of their velocities in an effort to determine which shot best and whether any should be avoided. This video shows all the results in real time and gives details on their relative performance.

All the loads were chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor. I chose the 6.5 Creed because it is today’s most popular big-game centerfire rifle cartridge; it is stocked everywhere from Alabama to Alaska; and, as the poster child of Modern Cartridge Design, it is inherently accurate and I wanted the ammo in this test to perform as well as possible.

I put each load through two different rifles. One is the Seekins SIC Short Action, a high-end precision rifle that I’ve been using extensively for the last year and is slated to be released to the public in 2027. The other is a Ruger American Rifle Gen II, one of the best all-around hunting rifles for those on a budget. We’ve been big fans of the Ruger American since it was introduced – it won an Editor’s Choice in our annual gun test when it debuted – and the platform continues to impress us with its combination of accuracy-enhancing features, good stock ergonomics, and smooth-cycling action.

I put 20 rounds of each whitetail ammo through each rifle for a total of 40 rounds per offering. I measured those 5-shot groups on my E.A.T.S. targets to come up with an average group size by rifle and then calculated the combined average group size of all eight groups through both rifles.

I captured velocity data on a Garmin Xero C2 Chronograph. The Garmin’s ability to stop and restart sessions allowed me to gather 20 shots of data with each gun and ammo combo for the velocity averages, extreme spreads (ES), and standard deviations (SD). With factory ammo, any 20-shot SD in the teens is very good and there’s nothing wrong with values in the 20s either, especially for the center-of-mass deer hunting ammo we’re showcasing here.

The results of the test were fascinating. The Winchester Deer Season XP and Barnes Harvest performed extremely well, Federal’s Fusion Tipped delivered very good precision, the Nosler Whitetail Country and Hornady American Whitetail loads were solid all around, and the Remington Core-Lokt Tipped gave mixed results that serve as a cautionary tale when selecting hunting ammo.

This data is based on the average of four 5-shot groups with each rifle and ammo combination. The combined value is the average of how the ammunition did in both the Seekins SIC SA and the Ruger American Rifle Gen II.

The muzzle velocity and standard deviation data is also based on 20 shots, except for the Federal 140-grain Fusion Tipped, which is based on 30 shots of data.

This is the most visually distinctive ammo in the test with Winchester’s oversized polymer tip that’s designed to produce violent and quick bullet upset upon impact.

This ammunition delivered the best groups overall, with a 5-shot average of .700 inches. The 20 shots through the Seekins averaged .652 inches, while the Ruger’s groups averaged .749 inches.

You can find it online for about $35 for a box of 20, but it is currently hard to find a vendor that has it in stock. The 125-grain version is available but wasn’t the load we tested so we can’t assume it will perform at the same level.

The Harvest Collection is the love child that resulted from the union of Barnes Bullets and Sierra Bullets, which were joined in corporate matrimony back in 2020. I’ve had excellent results with this ammunition, which was officially unveiled in April 2025, both in terms of its accuracy at the bench and its performance in the field.

The idea behind the Harvest Collection is simple. Barnes took Sierra’s well-regarded Tipped Game King bullet and loaded it in their brass on their machinery, which has a reputation for holding tight tolerances.

With an overall average 5-shot group size of .704 inches, it finished just behind Winchester in this evaluation. That said, I’ve had even better results with this ammunition in other rifles, such as my Sako TRG 22-A1. My groups through that rifle averaged .491 inches at 2692 fps with a 15.7 fps SD.

I’ve used this load on a few whitetails at this point, and the terminal results have been excellent too.

You can find the 6.5 Creedmoor load online for about $40 per box of 20.

The Fusion Tipped bullet has become a go-to of mine in the last couple of years not only for whitetails, but also antelope, elk and mule deer.

In terms of its construction, it falls between traditional cup-and-core projectiles and true bonded bullets with respect to its toughness. It’ll retain weight better than a non-bonded bullet but is cheaper to produce than a chemically bonded bullet and has the added benefit of being more inherently accurate than one, too.

In truth, the Fusion Tipped strikes a beautiful balance between accuracy, terminal performance, and economy. During this test the 140-grain Fusion Tipped averaged .989 inches in group size, with the Seekins turning in .784-inch groups and the Ruger delivering 1.194-inch groups.

I’ve found the 6.5 Creedmoor online for $46 to $50 per box, which makes it one of the more expensive whitetail-oriented ammo offerings. If that’s a bit rich for your blood, consider the traditional Fusion line, which can usually be found for a few dollars less per box.

The Nosler Solid Base bullet was first introduced more than half a century ago, but it never caught on like the company’s iconic Partition and Ballistic Tipped projectiles and there were years where the company halted production altogether.

But this cup-and-core soft point, with its tapered jacket, makes for a dandy hunting bullet for whitetails and other big game at moderate distances and it is enjoying a revival of sorts in Nosler’s Whitetail Country lineup.

The bullet’s accuracy in this test was solid. With 5-shot groups averaging 1.167 inches it is more than capable of taking deer at distances to 300 yards or more. Interestingly, this ammunition was the only one in the test where the budget-oriented Ruger American Rifle outshot my fancy-pants Seekins SIC. My four 5-shot groups from the Ruger averaged 1.131 inches, besting the Seekins which averaged 1.202 inches.

The 140-grain 6.5 Creed load goes for $33 to $40 per box of 20 online, making it one of the more affordable selections in the test.

Inside the jacket of this bullet is a raised ring that helps keep the lead core in place as it expands and penetrates within the target. That “locking” element gave the InterLock its name and it’s been part of the American hunting landscape for half a century now.

Loaded in the American Whitetail line, it is one of the most affordable bread-and-butter offerings for big-game hunters. The price per box hovers around $33 currently.

Its attractive price tag and its reasonable performance — through the two test rifles its average 5-shot group average measured 1.375 inches — earned it a Great Buy award in this round up.

This ammunition delivered the largest overall groups in the test, with a 5-shot average of 1.519 inches. On the surface, that’s mediocre performance, but it comes with a significant caveat.

The Ruger American Rifle Gen II did not care for this ammunition. The four 5-shot groups measured 2.065, 2.699, 2.392, and 2.143 inches, for an average of 2.325 inches. That isn’t a result I’d feel confident hunting with, and I doubt many of you would be satisfied with it either.

But through the Seekins SIC SA, the ammo hammered. Those four groups came in at 1.039, .595, .589, and .630 inches, averaging .713 inches overall. Across the 12 rifle and ammo combinations in the test that was third only to how well the Seekins shot the Barnes Harvest ammo at .642 inches and Winchester ammo at .652 inches.

The lessons here are that there’s no reason for you to go afield with substandard precision from a modern hunting rifle shooting quality modern ammunition, and that it pays to test out different loads when preparing for firearms season.

The Core-Lokt Tipped offering in 6.5 Creed runs around $43 online currently.

Investing in a few boxes of ammunition is all it takes to help your deer rifle reach its precision potential. Four 5-shot groups will yield more reliable data than three, but even 15 well-placed deliberate shots on target will give you a good feel for the performance of your system.

In any event, there’s no reason to head to your favorite stand or block of public ground with a nagging sense of uncertainty about how your rifle will shoot when that big buck steps into the clear.

As you can see from this evaluation, even with a budget-minded rig like the Ruger, you can have a true sub-MOA rifle if you take the time to figure out what your hunting rig likes.

#8296. We Tested the Viral ‘Slither Rig’ So You Don’t Have To

Published Nov 5, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

When it comes to bass fishing baits, the Slither Rig is the latest craze on social media. Half flipping bait, half saltwater spoon, this setup certainly raises an eyebrow at first glance. But when an urchin is the most effective lure for catching a bass, who’s to say a saltwater spoon couldn’t work, too? So I set out to try this new contraption, and here’s what I found.

The Slither Rig consists of three parts: a saltwater jigging spoon, a flipping hook, and a flipping bait. Any saltwater jigging spoon will do; I picked up a pack of five for about 12 bucks on Amazon. You’ll want the spoon to weigh at least an ounce, because you’ll essentially be using it as a flipping weight. Remove the hooks from the spoon and replace the back one with a 4/0 flipping hook. Then slide your soft-plastic bait onto the hook, rig it weedless, and you’re ready to go.

The idea behind the Slither Rig is that you replace the traditional bullet-style weight with a spoon and use the weight of that spoon to plunge your bait through thick vegetation. For this style of fishing, you’ll need an extra-heavy/fast flipping/punching rod that’s at least 7 feet, 8 inches long. Pair that rod with a reel with a 7:1 or higher gear ratio, and spool the combo with 65-pound or stronger braid.

I fished the Slither Rig intermittently over the course of three trips, totaling six or seven hours with it. Toward the end of my testing, I finally got a couple of bites flipping thick gator grass and hyacinth mats. But up until that point, I found the Slither Rig to be more trouble than it was worth.

My biggest frustration with the Slither Rig was its inability to punch cleanly through the mat. Granted, I was only using a 1-ounce spoon in areas where I would typically use a 1 1/2-ounce tungsten weight. But this chunk of metal was already as long as my bait, so I didn’t want to go any bigger for fear of increasing the risk of a fish hitting the spoon and missing the bait carrying the hook. And I’m not sure it would have mattered anyway. The issue had less to do with the weight of the setup and more to do with the way it hinged in the middle.

Nine times out of ten, when I flipped the Slither Rig out, it would land flat on the cover and then bend in the middle, causing both the bait and the spoon to catch on the cover. It was like trying to push an already-sprung drywall anchor into a hole in the wall. The physics just didn’t work.

I found that I could flip the bait higher and get it to go through a little better, but the kerplunk of it smacking the mat was off-putting to me and no doubt disturbing to any bass sitting in the foot or two of water beneath the mats. So I was left with no option but to flip the bait onto the mat and then gently jiggle it until it fell through, which worked about a third of the time.

Personally, I don’t see a situation in which the Slither Rig would ever be a better choice than a traditional punching setup. Yes, the spoon adds flash that could have some appeal in stained water, perhaps. But silver tungsten weights can do the same thing, and they punch through cover far more cleanly.

While I did manage to get a couple of bites on the Slither Rig, I have zero doubt that I could have caught more fish had I flipped a traditional pegged punching rig or Texas rig through all of the same areas, simply because I would have been able to present my bait to the bass better.

Is the Slither Rig legit? Practically speaking, no. You may see someone on facespace talking about how it’s the next big thing, but don’t let them fool you. While I did prove to myself that I could get bit on it, the mechanics of the setup just aren’t conducive to heavy cover. Consider this one debunked.

#8292. CDT Southern Terminus Closure Lifted, Border Monument To Be Relocated

The Continental Divide Trail’s southern terminus and southernmost mile have reopened following a temporary construction closure, according to the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC). This section of the trail had been closed in late October so that construction crews could widen an access road and construct a second border barrier at the terminus.

The first mile of the CDT falls within the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area (NDA), a military zone created in spring 2025 when roughly 110,000 acres along the US-Mexico border were transferred from the Bureau of Land Management into Army control. Hikers seeking to access the trail’s southern terminus must submit to a background check and obtain an Army permit. Noncitizens must also have a US citizen escort through the NDA who also has an access permit.

“These events are unprecedented in the history of our trail system: the transfer of a critically significant element of our national scenic trail into the Department of Defense control, the conversion of the CDT Southern Terminus into a military and construction zone of momentous scale, and trail management partnerships that include land management agencies and state governments, but also the US military,” the CDTC said in a press release.

The CDTC received word today from US Army officials at Fort Huachuca that the trail is once again officially open, although construction activities are ongoing and hikers may still encounter traffic, road closures, and delays in the area. “This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the organization said. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”

The press release also indicates that the construction of the second border wall means the southern terminus monument will need to be relocated to an area outside of the border walls, and that access to the monument may be temporarily prohibited during construction and relocation. “CDTC does not know the exact timing of the relocation but will provide updates as available,” the organization wrote.

#8290. The 3 Best Ways to Cook a Venison Backstrap

Published Nov 5, 2026 4:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I ate a lot of venison when I was a kid. Any recipe that could be made with beef, my mother made with deer meat — hamburgers, spaghetti sauce, pot roast, and more. However, she didn’t ever get too creative with venison backstraps. Although she realized they were a prized piece of meat, she mostly over-cooked them in a frying pan and then smothered them with gravy.

When I started harvesting my own deer, it felt like preparing a delicious meal was the best way to honor the animal. WIth a little culinary research and some experimentation in the kitchen, I learned that there are far tastier venison backstrap recipes for turning this prime cut into a meal. Here are some of my favorite ways to prepare a venison backstrap. These recipes were refined with whitetail meat, but they also work well for any big game animal.

The backstrap is a super lean and tender strip of meat that runs along a deer’s spine, stretching from the shoulder blades to the last vertebra. There are two backstraps, one on each side of the spine. Each one will weigh 1 to 3 pounds depending on the size of the deer.

The backstrap of a deer is equivalent to ribeye and filet mignon cuts from cattle. However, venison backstraps are much leaner than beef ribeye. It is a coveted cut of meat best served medium rare (between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit). When cooked to a higher temp than that, the meat quickly turns from tender and juicy to dry and chewy.

When it comes off the deer, the backstrap is covered in a layer of connective tissue often referred to as “silver skin.” When exposed to heat, the silver skin becomes very tough. Remove the silver skin before cooking. Here’s how:

Because backstrap is such an inherently delicious and tender cut of meat, it doesn’t really need any elaborate preparations. Sometimes simple is better. It lets the natural taste really shine through. You could even serve just the steaks alone without the mushrooms and onions.

You can really fancy-fy your venison backstrap recipe with this twist on traditional Wellington. The process is long, but the rewards are well worth the effort. Serve with roasted potatoes and winter veggies.This recipe is relatively complicated and has lots of steps. If it seems confusing, check out this step-by-step guide to beef Wellington by Gordon Ramsey. We’re essentially doing the same thing—but with venison and without the accent.

The key to any delicious venison backstrap recipe is to not overcook. Although the loin is naturally tender and juicy, it can turn tough and dry in a hurry with too much exposure to heat. The best venison backstrap will still be plenty pink in the middle.

#8288. Bowhunter Tags Massive 191-Inch Buck That’s Somehow Still in Velvet

Published Nov 6, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jackson Berner was at work when one of his remote trail cameras captured a photo of a giant velvet buck the morning of October 20. The 21-year-old commercial insulator was on the job in southwest Ohio when he got the early morning picture of the deer near his hunting treestand.

“I said ‘Holy Smoke’ when I saw the size of the deer and its velvet,” Berner tells Outdoor Life. “The buck came by my camera at 7:50 a.m., and I’d never seen it before.”

Berner wanted to be in his treestand the following morning in case the buck happened to walk by the spot again.

“I asked my boss if I could have the next day off to hunt,” Berner says. “I showed him photos of the buck, and he said to go and get that deer.”

The following morning on Oct. 21, Berner was 22 feet up a tree sitting in a lock-on stand near where his trail camera had gotten photos of the velvet buck the previous morning.

“My brother-in-law told me he believed I was gonna shoot that buck,” explains Berner, of Springfield, Ohio. “I just had a feeling I’d get that deer, too.”

He climbed into his treestand just as it was nearing legal shooting light, a bit after 7 a.m.

“Legal shooting time was 7:22 a.m., and the velvet buck showed up at 7:30, like the previous day,” he says. “The velvet buck had been with a smaller buck on camera the first day I had photos of him. I first saw the little 4-point buck on the trail that morning, and not far behind him was the big buck.”

When the big deer got closer it stopped and looked up directly at the hunter.

“I froze, and when he dropped his head and walked a few steps, I drew my bow and took the shot at 15 yards.”

His 62-pound Darton bow sent an arrow tipped with a G5 Megameat 3-blade expandable broadhead. The arrow hit home and passed through.

“My adrenaline was on fire, as I watched him run out of sight about 60 yards away,” Berner says. “I decided to leave the woods and come back in an hour with some help to track my deer.”

Berner returned with his father Jason, cousin and brother-in-law. It was an easy-to-follow blood trail, and the party found the deer dead only 50 yards beyond from where Berner had lost sight of it that morning.

They loaded the deer into a Polaris side-by-side and then started field dressing the deer.

“We got to looking at him for gutting and thought perhaps it had no testicles, which is common for late-season velvet bucks,” Berner says. “But he had his man parts. The only thing we could figure is his testes had been injured somehow, and that resulted in him keeping his velvet so late in the year.”

Read Next: Here’s Why This Giant Missouri Buck Was Still in Velvet in Late September

Berner took his velvet buck to Toby Hughes, a popular Buckmasters scorer who measured the 16-pointer rack at 191 inches. Hughes says it’s one of the biggest velvet bucks ever taken in Ohio.

Berner delivered his deer to a meat processor, and the butcher told him he found a bullet in the deer’s hindquarters. Berner says the deer showed no signs of having been shot previously, and its hide was completely healed over.

“One other thing about that buck, is when I spotted it first on my trail camera, it was near where my fiance and I are planning to get married,” Berner says. “That’s pretty amazing.”

#8285. Here’s Why the Classic Buck Knife Is the Only Deer Gutting Blade I’ll Ever Need

Published Nov 6, 2026 11:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A few weeks ago, I broke out my sharpener and got my Buck knife ready for another long season. This is an annual ritual, and each year I take a moment to admire the wear and tear the blade and handle have seen. Each little blemish tells its own story, and for this knife, it holds every story of my hunting career.

I received this knife when I began hunting which, here in Pennsylvania, kicked off when I was 12 years old. Back then, the knife was new, shiny, and sharper than I could ever get it to be now. But more important than the aesthetics of the knife was its potential. I had no idea what it would help me accomplish in the next 17 hunting seasons.

I know that large, fixed blade knives like this one are not trendy in the hunting world. Everyone seems to be moving to smaller blades with fancier steels or ultra-light and ultra-sharp replaceable-blade knives. But the truth is, you don’t need an expensive precision instrument to gut a deer. For me, it’s a lot more meaningful to use a knife that has so many good memories scratched into it than a new high-end blade.

And that, among a few other reasons, is why I believe the Buck knife will live forever.

In 1902 Hoyt Buck, a 13-year-old blacksmith’s apprentice in Kansas, was experimenting with ways to temper steel so it would keep an edge for longer. He was, of course, successful in his experiment, although the Buck knife didn’t show up in the market for years after Buck’s discovery.

In 1947, Hoyt and his son Alfred set up a shop called H.H. Buck & Son behind their home. The father and son duo continued to make high-quality hand made knives and their business took off. In fact, Hoyt Buck made approximately 25 knives by hand each week until his death in 1949.

Alfred Buck then took over where his father left off. In the early 50s, he expanded advertising of Buck knives to mail order catalogs. In 1961, Buck was incorporated and in 1964, the company introduced the Model 110 Folding Hunter knife, which became one of the most popular knives ever made. In 1992, Buck debuted the Nighthawk, a fixed-blade knife that was 6.5 inches and had a black handle made of Zytel for an ergonomic grip. This knife was submitted to the U.S. Navy for evaluation for use by Navy Seals.

With over 100 years of blacksmithing and knife work under the Buck name’s belt, it’s no wonder why they’re still one of the most popular knife producers to this day.

While my Buck knife isn’t the original Model 110 Folding Hunter, it still carries a traditional feel to it. My Buck 119 Special fixed blade knife has some quality components, and admittedly does leave some room for improvements too.

The 6-inch blade is made from 420HC steel and is clipped into a phenolic handle. In total, the knife weighs 7.5 ounces. It’s heavy, bulky, and not always easy to maneuver, but it sure does work. It’s great for that first cut while field dressing a deer because the tip curves, allowing my hand to drop down lower than the tip to avoid puncturing the stomach or other intestines during the process.

Where it seems to fall short in comparison to newer, fancier knives are the close-quarters work above the diaphragm when removing the heart and lungs. The large blade is often difficult to twist and turn in the tight space, leading to a few accidental knicks to my fingers from time to time.

When I compared it with a new Montana Knife Company Whitetail knife, I was able to see just how much more convenient it is to have a smaller, 4” blade for maneuverability in the body cavity. I’ll be doing a full side-by-side comparison between the two knives in the coming weeks, so more on that later.

I’m not sure if it’s because I’m getting older or what, but recalling all of the memories this knife and I have shared really hit home this year. We’ve come a long way together. This knife has been there for all of the “firsts” in my hunting career: My first deer, first buck, first turkey, and even my first bear. It’s been on out-of-state hunts, out-of-country hunts, and even got lost in the prairie of South Dakota for a day or two after it gutted my first mule deer.

Sometimes it’s so dull from running into bone that it couldn’t cut a piece of paper, while other times, I’ve kept the edge so keen it’s like running a knife through butter. It hasn’t lived a glamorous life, but it’s been there for each of the moments I truly live for.

After chatting with OL’s executive gear editor Scott Einsmann and realizing that many hunters don’t have the same knife they started with, I called my Dad to tell him we might just be a tad weird. You see, I can’t claim that I’m the one who started this “same knife forever” trend. My Dad has been running the same gutting knife in his deer hunting pack for over 43 years.

After running my Buck knife through the WorkSharp a few times, I felt the edge to make sure it was ready for another year being lugged around the deer woods with me. There are, admittedly, a few burrs that I need to address if I want it to be perfect, but it’s good enough for me. The knife may not be perfect, but it’s perfect for me.

I packed it away in its black sheath and tucked it into my hunting pack, hoping it would see the light of day in a few short weeks. As luck would have it, opening week was quite successful, and the knife gutted a doe for me, and a first archery buck for a close friend. After a quick rinse and another few rounds in the WorkSharp, it’s right back where it belongs, in my pack, ready for our next adventure.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8284. Cozy Bed to Selden Pass — John Muir Trail Day 15

After last night’s fabulous dinner, I expected to sleep like a baby.  And I did.  For a while.

Then a very disturbing event occurred, relating to my left wrist injury.  I woke up in the middle of the night and my thumb, index finger, third finger and fourth finger were completely and totally numb on my left hand, and the pinky was partially numb.

I hoped (fervently!) that this only meant I had slept on my injured wrist in a bad way.  The alternative would seem to be nerve damage of some kind.  Of the kind that says, “Get off the trail right away and see a doctor!!”

Gradually I managed to get feeling back.  As it slowly returned, I was cautiously relieved.  But I recognized that if the extreme numbness came back, then it was not a random misfortune, but something I really needed to worry about.  Aside from possible long-term damage, hiking with no feeling in my left hand was out of the question.

The other change overnight was temperature.  When I turned in, it was hot, even stuffy in my little cabin home, so I went to sleep with just my shirt on, with bare feet and bare legs.  There was no top sheet on the bed, just a sheet on the mattress and a blanket.  So, I slept between the sheet and the blanket.

Over the course of the night, it started to get ever chillier.  As the night went on, I added my little knit cap; then I added socks.  As it cooled further, I got out my sleeping bag liner and hopped in.  Finally, I got my puffy jacket and wrapped it around my legs and eventually that seemed to do the trick.  I was extremely resistant to pulling out my sleeping bag, I did not want to do that if I could help it.  Somehow that would have made the overnight feel less like a true break from the trail, I guess.

When I got up in the morning, my fingers all still had sensation, they were moving.  My wrist was still injured, but my fear of nerve damage abated.

I went up to breakfast and oh what a spread!  This is a place that serves hikers. They had scrapple, bacon, pancakes, eggs, fruit, yogurt, and coffee, of course.  The same crew from the night before all sat around and we stuffed our faces, understandably, as hungry hikers are prone to do.

Smiles showed me a picture of the inside of her cabin from the night before and it was hilarious!

With a great fear of SPIDERS, Smiles had set up and slept in her tent INSIDE her MTR cabin!

This picture gives a good sense of how she obtained her trail name!

So that’s what retired New York oncologists look like!

Lauralyn was there too, and she said, ”You know, you said you were going to recite that poem, how about it?”

Lauralyn encouraging me to recite The Raven

I warned them all it would take more than ten minutes and they said, “That’s okay, go ahead.”

As everyone was getting served, and kitchen staff were moving through the room, I recited The Raven.  They said they really enjoyed it, and I think they did.  With the distractions in the room, it was probably not my best performance, but I did all right.

It was time to get going, so I got my resupply bucket that was stashed in the kitchen under lock and key for bear protection.  Shlepping it to my cabin it felt very heavy.  Then I opened it and there was so much stuff I didn’t need.  I began sorting – everything I wanted went on the bed for packing, everything I did not went back in the bucket.

Smiles dropped by and told me, “I extended, I’m gonna stay here another day.”

“Okay, fine,” I replied, adding, “you know, I’m so tempted to go up to the dining area and fill one of my water bottles with their lemonade!”

She said, “Come on, I’m going that way anyway, let’s go.”

Together we went up.  Maybe my plan was perfectly acceptable, but it helped to have a partner in crime.  I filled up on lemonade, and it proved so delicious on the trail, I enjoyed it so much.

While near the dining room I used the flush toilet, the only one on their whole property.  It didn’t seem like a big deal, but I wanted to get my money’s worth.  (It was $375 a night, remember?)

Unfortunately, I never went in the hot spring, and the people who believe in those things were just raving about it.  The day before, when I might have done it, they had girls cleaning it with toothbrushes and I just didn’t feel like it any other time.

Back in the cabin, I finished packing, surprised that almost all my food fit in the bear canister.  It seemed I was getting a bit more efficient at that task.  My charger block almost got fully charged, finally, so that was good news too.

Before leaving Muir Trail Ranch, I dropped off my plastic five-gallon  bucket full of not-needed items (mostly food) at the reception location.   Just at that moment a German couple arrived and said, “Oh we forgot to send food, we have no food.”

I replied, “Well this is your lucky day, there’s a ton of food in here.  It’s good, expensive food too.”  It was, because a lot of it was the pricey freeze-dried stuff.  Somehow, I had badly miscalculated.  Whatever the reason, that couple made out like bandits.  The adage, “the trail provides” was certainly true for them that day!

I was facing a long uphill, over 3,000 feet to cross Selden Pass, and the very first stretch was one of the steepest.  After a break, when you first start walking, especially uphill, and when your pack is heavy from resupply, your legs can feel like lead.  Mine felt that way, for sure, but the good news was, it didn’t last long.

Pretty soon I was going up at a good pace, but I was stuck behind a horse being ridden by next-door-cabin Jay, who was behind a horse ridden by his guide.  Oddly, my pace was pretty close to that of the horses, but I didn’t want to get in front and hold them up.  At the same time, walking behind I was breathing the dust they were kicking up, so I kept having to drop back to get clear of that.

Finally, there was some separation between us.  The ascent included a lot of long switchbacks, so that the “crow fly” distance to MTR was not that great.  I could even still see it, just far, far beneath me now.  My blood was really pumping from all the uphill!

I was pleased at how I handled it.  True, it was at a lower elevation, but I thought at last I might be getting my trail legs.  Soon I crossed over some forests and meadows and was out of sight of the resort.  I spotted some wildflowers by the trail.

Perhaps it was the season, but I did not see the profusion of wildflowers on the JMT I have seen on other trails

In one of the meadows I was puzzled.  There was a path straight across, but someone had blocked it off.  As I skirted the glade, following the detour, I came across the team building the trail on more sustainable ground, to preserve the fragile meadow.   These folks do such an important job, making the trail better for all of us, and getting paid rather small salaries for doing it.  As always I stopped and thanked them profusely.  I wanted them to know that they and their work were deeply appreciated.

I came to the twin Sallie Keyes lakes.  As I arrived, I crossed some steppingstones over the exit creek and saw a beautiful snake swimming in the water; a garter snake, I think.  I even got its picture.

Right after this shot I watched the snake enter the water and swim away

Feeling hungry, I was tempted to have lunch there.  But then I looked at the map, and saw that the last lake before Selden Pass was called Heart Lake, because it’s shaped like a heart.

I thought, “That seems very appropriate. I will go to Heart Lake and have my lunch.”  At Muir Trail Ranch breakfasts they also lay out the fixings for making and packing a lunch.  I had prepared a sandwich and packed it into my Nalgene soaking container.  I also brought a fresh apple.

When I got to Heart Lake, I took off my shoes and socks, dunked my bare feet into the lake, and ate half of my sandwich.  Under the dry surface of the moss I was sitting on, the lower portion was very wet, meaning my shorts were quickly soaked.

The moss is where I sat and the water is where I swam

As I realized how wet my seat was, I also realized the thought of a swim was very attractive.  So, I took off my clothes, put on my water shoes, and walked into Heart Lake.  I plunged my whole body in, swam out my usual 10 yards, then swam back.  It refreshed me so much.  And yes, I was skinny dipping, except for my water shoes.

But nobody came by while I was swimming.  Afterwards I dried off a little bit and put my damp shorts back on.  Then I ate the rest of my sandwich and my apple and finished off the MTR lemonade.  It was so good.  I’d been drinking it all day, climbing and climbing.  Now it was gone.

A little hard to see, but those are the two upper lobes of the “heart” that names Heart Lake

Energized by food and swim, I continued on up to Selden Pass.  It was a little weird, because no one else was there.  Usually when you get to a pass, you are not alone.  It seems people get to a pass, and they often stay there for a while.  The are resting, or eating, or just enjoying the view and celebrating their accomplishment on top of the world.  Sam and I crossed Forrester Pass alone, but that day the weather was challenging, so nobody stayed up there.

On Selden Pass I was alone, and it was nice to be there by myself.  Then I started down, realizing it was now around 3.30 p.m., which meant my progress was faster than I expected.  That morning I envisioned arriving at closer to 5:00 p.m.  It seemed I was in better shape than I thought.

View north from Selden Pass, the lake is Marie Lake

Descending I was trying to balance going pretty fast, while also being careful to avoid another accident.  As I  proceeded down, I met a couple of women and, in the course of the discussion, one of them revealed their hike was a birthday trip.

So, I asked the birthday girl her name (Sydney) and I sang “Happy Birthday dear Sydney” to her.  That’s just what I do.

Further down I met a woman, an American of Korean origin, who was just finishing a (very late!) lunch at a stream.  She told me her trail name was Ninja Queen because she is allergic to UV light and therefore wears a ninja’s face mask and bright reflector sunglasses.

Just then another couple came going southbound and she too was Korean and was even carrying a Korean flag!   She said some Korean guys had a bunch of extra flags and offered  her one.  She felt patriotic and said, “Okay, sure!”

The guy she was with had the trail name Eminem.  It seemed they had met on trail and were just friends.  We took a selfie of the four of us meeting on the trail.

Papa George, Flag Girl, Eminem, and Ninja Queen hiking the High Sierra!

Such a random coincidence, right?  I said she should take “Flag Girl” as her trail name.  But it didn’t seem to really appeal to her.

I proceeded down and down and down, trying to make up as much distance as possible, so that tomorrow’s trip to VVR, Vermilion Valley Resort, is a relatively short one.  I did stop to refill my water at a stream crossing, and Ninja Queen passed me while I was there.  We exchanged greetings and found we both intended to overnight at VVR on the following day.

Finally, I got to the tent site that I was targeting.  To my disappointment, it appeared packed full.  I walked up to a tent to ask if there were any spots available nearby, and it was Sally!  The news about spaces was not hopeful, but I enjoyed stopping and chatting with her briefly.  That was very nice, especially when she said, “Yeah, all day I was asking, where is George? Where do you think George is?”

When I admitted I left MTR at 10:00 a.m. she went, “You left at 10 o’clock???”  Only then did I feel a little abashed at my late start.

That campsite was full, then the next campsite was full too.  The sun was getting lower and finally dropped behind the ridge.  It was still light enough to see, but it was quickly darkening.  Finally, the third place was empty!  I found a spot that seemed adequate in the fading light and set up camp.  I soaked and then ate an al pastor rice dish that was actually good, and I hid my bear cannister.  It was too dark by then to think about digging a cathole.

My faithful Big Agnes tent in the campsite near the river

Then I settled in for another night in the woods.

In my 69 years I’ve done a lot of cool things – I’ve crossed the Atlantic in a 40-foot sailboat, bushwacked 100 miles across the north slope of the Alaska Range, hiked for 26 days in Western Nepal crossing five passes over 5,000 meters, and climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. I have been active in retirement, and I hiked the Wonderland Trail in 2024 and the Long Trail in 2025. This year I'm trying... the John Muir Trail!

#8281. Feds Unveil Plan to Overhaul National Wildlife Refuges, Get More ‘Boots on the Ground’

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:06 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Following a 6-month review of the operation, purpose, and function of America’s National Wildlife Refuges, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service today announced an initiative to improve habitat, expand refuge access, and redirect resources to field operations.

Results of the internal refuge review were greeted with relief by wildlife organizations, some of which worried that the Trump administration intended to divest some refuges or to weaken their role as America’s top-tier wildlife properties.

In comments this morning at the Audubon NWR in North Dakota, both Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum and USFWS Director Brian Nesvik outlined 29 recommendations that generally support refuge field operations, improve both public access and administrative efficiency, and boost law enforcement resources.

However, with a 20 percent cut in funding and the loss of nearly a third of its workforce, it’s unclear how the Service will implement some of today’s directives.

The recommendations announced today are compiled in a program called Rooted In Purpose that generally increases the Department of Interior’s investments in the National Wildlife Refuge System that includes 573 refuges across 95 million acres of land. Nesvik announced the initiative in December 2025 and tapped fellow Wyomingite and senior advisor Joshua Coursey to conduct the 6-month review. Nesvik further detailed the background and sideboards of the refuge review in a wide-ranging interview with Outdoor Life in January 2026.

“Our purpose is simply to confirm that [each] refuges’ original purpose still aligns with the Service’s current mission,” Nesvik told Outdoor Life in January. “People have assumed that means we’re looking for ways to sell land. That is not the intent. The intent is to make sure we’re still doing those things that were intended when the refuge was created but also to make sure that things aren’t completely askew from our current mission.”

Today’s announcement, which is also detailed in a Secretarial Order entitled “Making America’s National Wildlife Refuges Great Again” issued by Burgum, distilled the 6-month review into four main areas of focus that the Service will apply over the next two years.

Nesvik noted today that his Director’s Order 230 resulted in 41 in-person refuge visits, 118 virtual visits, and four regional office visits along with internal surveys that solicited more than 1,000 responses from USFWS staff, and an external survey that received more than 2,000 responses.

“Refuge employees know what the land needs and what it takes to get the work done,” Nesvik said today in remarks delivered at the North Dakota refuge. “Their experience shaped this review, and their input will help us put its recommendations into action. We are focused on giving them practical tools and clear guidance to manage habitat, protect wildlife and provide Americans with quality hunting, fishing and other outdoor opportunities.”

Today’s news was generally welcomed by wildlife organizations.

“The USFWS refuge system has been an important part of the conservation successes in North America,” said Corey Mason, CEO and executive vice president of conservation for the Wild Sheep Foundation. “We applaud Secretary Burgum and Director Nesvik’s efforts to refocus the refuge system on the field work necessary to ensure quality habitat for wildlife and opportunity for Americans to benefit from that work and access these unique places.”

Ariel Weigard, vice president for government affairs for Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever commended Burgum and Nesvik “for their efforts to strengthen the National Wildlife Refuge System and its ability to deliver conservation on the ground.”

Today’s announcement didn’t detail how the Rooted in Purpose initiative will be funded and implemented. The USFWS budget has been cut by about 20 percent, or some $323 million in the Trump administration’s 2027 budget. Programs that have been either cut or eliminated next year include state and tribal wildlife grants, migratory bird conservation funds, and the entire National Wildlife Refuge Fund.

The Rooted in Purpose program provides some insights in how funding might be redirected to achieve the goals of refuge reform. The document details the Service intends to eliminate the Urban Wildlife Conservation Program Policy and “redirect all discretionary program funding to activities that directly support the conservation mission.”

The directive also prioritizes what it calls “boots on the ground.”

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Land Is Worse Than You Thought

“Reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources.”

Lastly, the Service intends to stretch limited resources by using “technology and Super Intelligence to improve efficiency” and to promote contracting and reducing barriers for “for qualified local businesses competing for federal work.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.
