#8278. The Best Gifts for Hunters: Get Them What They Actually Want

Published Nov 6, 2026 1:22 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Hunters can present a challenge when it comes to gift buying. They already have one of these or two of those. They don’t particularly care for Model A or Brand B. There’s always the $100 Gift Card, but you really don’t want to be that impersonal, now do you?

Fortunately, there’s an almost endless array of “I’d love one of those” gift ideas whether the hunter on your list chases waterfowl, big game, upland birds, or small game. This year, the following gift ideas will help you put the right hunting gear beneath the tree.

Missing a target means lost or broken arrows. Not only does that get expensive, it’s downright discouraging. The BlackOut LongShot 36 is a big target that allows bowhunters to confidently practice shooting their bows at extended ranges without worrying about missing the target. Best of all, it’s affordable. In my testing, I’ve found arrow removal is easy, even though I’m shooting small-diameter arrows over 290 fps.

Even if you’re shopping for a bowhunter who already owns a backyard target, they’ll still want and need this one. It’s a can’t-miss gift for anyone who loves flinging arrows.

Thermal monoculars are handy devices to have around the house and in the field. They can help you locate coyotes in the pitch dark, blood trail a deer (where legal) and make home repairs, such as finding heat leaking out of a window. The key to choosing a thermal as a gift is understanding that the more you spend, the better the image gets. But not all use cases require top-end performance. If someone is going to use their thermal to scan fields, recover game, and use around the property, a lower-resolution sensor works well. If they need to view and identify animals at longer ranges (beyond 100 yards), they’ll need a top-of-the-line unit.

The ATN BlazeSeeker 6 is a compact thermal that slips easily into a pocket and can record photos and videos. It costs only $429 to $489 and is ideal for everyday use around the property and in the field. If you’re buying for someone who needs more capability, I recommend the BlazeTrek 6. The BlazeTrek 6 has a better image and costs $795 to $1,499. Both monoculars are easy to use, and the ATN app has a handy AI assistant to guide you through any snags the recipient might encounter. Any hunter will be thrilled to receive an ATN monocular, and it’s another fantastic gift to consider.

Good gifts are practical, but the best gifts help people have fun. One of the keys to having fun in the outdoors is being comfortable no matter the conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket is a highly versatile, packable layer that’s ideal for staying outside when the weather turns cold. From fishing to late-season hunting, this is an outer shell that will get a ton of use. We’ve tested and recommended the Foundry Jacket. You can read our full review to learn more.

Soft cases are the practical way to carry a shotgun to the range or to your hunting spot. They’re something that every bird hunter needs and will use regularly. They’re also relatively affordable, which makes them a great gift. The Evolution Outdoor Rawhide Classic Camo Shotgun Case is a stylish and practical case that’s made from waxed canvas. It will carry shotguns up to 50 inches in overall length, so it will accommodate most semi-automatics with 28-inch or shorter barrels and double guns with up to 30-inch barrels.

It’s tough buying the right knife for an outdoorsman, but you can’t go wrong with the iconic Victorinox Huntsman made by the folks who produced the original Swiss Army Knife™. The Huntsman has 15 functions, including blades, corkscrew, reamer, punch and sewing awl, scissors, wood saw, wire stripper, screwdrivers, and more. It’s available in 7 different color patterns. You can be sure that the outdoorsman on your list will find unlimited uses for this versatile Swiss-made tool through the many seasons that it will serve them.

Built to handle rough roads, bad weather, and air travel, this is a gift that tells someone you understand their passion and want to protect the tools that make it possible. It’s designed to hold two scoped rifles, with thick protective foam inside and six sturdy latches that keep everything sealed tight. Whether you’re shopping for a hunter that drives to the deer camp or flies out west for elk season, this case gives them peace of mind that their firearms will arrive zeroed and ready to hunt.— Scott Einsmann

You can get a turkey hunter a new call, a knife, or this piece of turkey hunting culture. The Tenth Legion is a book that captures the heart of what it is to be a diehard turkey hunter and is guaranteed to be enjoyed by anyone that chases gobbles throughout the spring. It was written by the legendary Colonel Tom Kelly, who recently passed on. I keep a copy of the Tenth Legion in my vest and read through it when the birds aren’t feeling talkative, and I highly recommend it as a gift for the turkey obsessed. — Scott Einsmann

Securely packaging your hard-won wild game, be it fresh venison, wild turkey, or mallard duck breasts has never been as easy as it is now, thanks to Cabela’s Deluxe 12 (D12) vacuum sealer. Weighing just four pounds, the D12 features a heavy-duty commercial vacuum pump designed for years of service. User-friendly, easy-to-clean, and programmable, the D12 takes up little counter space, while offering multiple modes of operation including manual seal, pulse, Auto/Vac, Standard, and Extended, as well as ‘Canister’ option great for preserving tough-to-seal foodstuffs.

This chest pack is designed to hold a hunter’s binoculars, and much much more. For backcountry hunters, a chest pack is a critical piece of gear and there are few out there that offer more features than the Kuiu Pro. It includes: magnetic closure for maximum quietness, adjustable main pouch for proper bino fit, rail-lock system for bottom accessory, rail-lock mount for ammo holder, plus a variety of extra pockets. It comes in five different camo/solid color options (I don’t think you can go wrong with solid Ash). This is an ideal gift for a big game hunter or even a turkey hunter, who needs quick access to optics and other critical gear.

A cellular trail camera is a perfect gift for any deer or turkey hunter. If the hunter already has a cell cam, they’ll be happy to have another (you can never have too many cameras out there). And if they don’t have camera yet, then your gift will get them in the game. And there’s not a trail camera out there that’s more effective and easy to use than the Tactacam 4.0. The Outdoor Life crew thoroughly tests trail cams every year, and the Tactacam 4.0 won the editor’s choice award, hands down, in 2026. Features include: Up to 4K photo definition, up to 96 feet of flash range, Low-glow or no-glow flash settings, 16 gb of internal storage, powered by 12 AA batteries, live video, on-demand photos, GPS enabled.

Sure, the description says ‘Waterfowl Backpack,’ and all duck hunters should have one of these, but don’t let the name fool you. This well-built large capacity pack has 101 uses in the field, e.g. camera bag, lunch box, blind bag, and dry clothes storage to name just a handful. With over 1,550 cubic inches of interior space, the Northern Flight backpack is crafted of rugged 600D polyester with a water-resistant polyurethane coating to help keep what’s inside nice and dry. There’s plenty of pockets, glove-friendly zippers, a huge main compartment, hydration pouch, and MOLLE attachment points for additional capacity. In other words this is an excellent hunting pack for a variety of scenarios.

How many times have you wished for some warmth while waiting out that trophy whitetail from inside the chilly confines of that late January ground blind? Thanks to the innovative minds at TideWe and their heated hunting chair, turning up the thermostat just became possible. At first glance, the chair seems ordinary enough – adjustable height; swiveling through 360 degrees; armrests; and a detachable gear pouch. But this chair adds a little spice in the form of battery-powered heat. Three heat levels (100 through 130 degrees), long 10-hour  battery life at the lowest setting, and a fast three-hour charge time make this ‘hot seat’ a Must-Have this winter.

Hunters constantly need to keep knives and broadheads sharp. This folding field sharpener is a versatile and handy way to maintain everything from pocketknives to axes. It’s only $13, and I’ve been testing it while sharpening broadheads and honing knives. It works great, and I recommend it.

*I noticed this product has only a three-star rating from customer reviews. But the reviews are all for a fishing reel. This appears to be a glitch on the Bass Pro Shops/Cabela’s website.

There’s nothing worse than slipping your feet into cold wet boots. Fortunately, the folks at PEET Dryer have the answer in their original boot dryer. The PEET dryer uses convection to push warm air upwards through specially designed chambers and ports to dry shoes and boots of all shapes, sizes, and material types. Safe enough to operate 24/7, this makes the perfect gift for anyone who goes outside, but especially hunters who are prone to get their boots wet.

Hunters often like to forage while they’re in the field. But wild mushrooms are nothing to be guessed at when it comes to their edibility. Some make wonderful meals, while others can make a person terribly sick, or worse. This makes a good mushroom identification book an absolute necessity for the forestland forager. And few are as comprehensive as David Arora’s All That The Rain Promises, and More. An educator in the field of mycology, Arora’s easy to understand descriptive prose, along with his excellent photographs, takes much of the mystery out of separating the ‘good’ from the ‘not so good’ when it comes to fungi.

Virtually indestructible. That’s the best way to describe YETI’s latest introduction, the Loadout Gobox 1 Gear Case. Built out of what the company refers to as ‘Defender II Material,’ the Gobox 1 is the perfect hard case if you’re looking to safely store items such as a wallet, passport, keys, portable power, or anything else. The Gobox 1 seals out Mother Nature, while providing roughly 56 cubic inches of interior space, yet only weighing 1.7 pounds. The Gobox 1 is ideal for kayakers, rafting enthusiasts, off-roaders, mountain bikers, and of course, hunters. And it’s available in five different colors.

There are about 101 different ways to repel mosquitoes but few are as effective and easy to use as a ThermaCELL. The lightweight MR300 uses a cylindrical fuel canister to gently warm a small metal plate, which in turn activates the material infused into the unit’s repellent mat. This repellent diffuses into a 15 square-foot zone of protection around the unit, keeping mosquitoes at bay within 15 minutes and (under optimal conditions) for as long as four hours. No batteries. No DEET sprays. And it’s safe to use around pets.

Firearm maintenance should be a concern of all hunters. Fortunately, the Allen Company’s Breakthrough Clean Technologies Universal Cleaning Kit helps make the job much easier. Included in the tough ammo can container are a variety of nylon brushes, brass patch jags, two multi-section cleaning rods, patches, swabs, a silicone gun cloth, solvent, and a bottle of ‘Battle Born’ high purity gun oil. It’s everything you need to clean a gun in one place.

Even in these modern times of precision air rifles, there’s still something to be said about Old School stuff — like Crosman’s 760 Pumpmaster air rifle. Now here’s a tool developed specifically to introduce young or new shooters to the shooting sports. The 760 handles both .177 caliber pellets and BBs, sending them downrange at 615/700 and 645 feet-per-second, respectively. A crossbolt safety, synthetic stock/fore-end, grooved receiver to accommodate a 4x scope, and traditional front/rear blade sights make this the perfect gift for all ages.

#8275. The 12 Best Riflescopes We Tested this Year: All Our Optics Test Winners

Published Nov 6, 2026 2:53 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Optics are one the most intensive and expansive categories we tackle. It’s a category we’ve been testing for as long as

This year we conducted two in-depth rifle scope tests. We kicked off the year in south Texas at the Thermal Ranch where we tested the latest in thermal scope technology while hunting hogs, predators, and shooting on the range. Then we met in eastern Montana to evaluate hunting scopes, LPVOs, and precision scopes. We tested them for their lowlight capability, tracking, ergonomics, overall shoot-ability, and we even drop tested them.

I encourage you to read our various in-depth scope buying guides: Best Hunting Scopes, Best Thermal Scopes, Best LPVOs, and Best Scopes for Deer Hunting. But, if you want a summary of just the award winners, this guide is for you. Below you’ll find the top performers from this year’s optics tests.

With this big, bright, and surprisingly sophisticated R7, Bushnell is restoring its relevance as a first-order hunting optic brand. The first focal-plane scope has an open tree-style reticle that’s anchored by an illuminated segmented circle and floating center dot that enables precision work as well as fast holdover and wind-informed shots at game.

For hunters and target shooters who would rather dial, the pull-to-turn elevation turret is nicely indexed and moves with positivity. The windage dial is capped.

Bushnell has invested heavily in the R7 line, which is the best of the Good/Better/Best product-line hierarchy that started with the R3 a couple years ago and continued with the R5 last year. The company has four different configurations of the R7, released just this month: a 1-8×24 LPVO, a 2-10×42, and a 3-15×50 in addition to the 4-20×50. The lower magnification scopes are available in second-plane reticles, but the two higher-mag versions come in either first- or second-plane reticles and either MIL or MOA, giving buyers a crazy number of variations on the platform.

We tested the second-plane MOA version of the 4-20×50, but for its versatility, performance on a wide range of targets and distances, and its flawless handling, we named the FFP R7 not only best Bushnell in the test, but the best overall hunting scope in the field of 25 excellent competitors. They include Nightforce’s new NX6, Leupold’s VX-4HD, and Zeiss’s new V3 families, along with some excellent submissions from Vortex, Trijicon, and Burris.

For its overall performance, the Bushnell R7 4-20×50 is this year’s Editor’s Choice winner as the top hunting scope of 2026.

The scope stacked points with a combination of good ED Prime glass, clear indexing on its controls, tight and positive turret and focus controls, and an illuminated Hybrid Dot Tree reticle that splits the difference between a precision competition and a hunting reticle. Its zero stop, which we’re glad to see on this type scope, is a 6-screw affair that’s a hassle to set, but works wonderfully as a solid backstop on elevation turret travel.

We worried about the durability of the R7, but it passed our inaugural drop test without skipping a beat. We dropped the scope three times from three feet on concrete covered by a 2-inch pad, and the Bushnell retained its zero.

Of course, our test teased out some deficiencies. The reticle references aren’t especially visible until about 7x, and I’d like to see one or two more intensity steps to the center-dot and segmented circle illumination to make them pop in daylight.

But if you’re looking for a rimfire or long-range competition scope that you can easily transition into a big-game hunt, this is a wonderful choice. The price, at about $950, is fair for the versatility and fine handling of this true crossover scope.

Read Next: The Best Riflescopes for Hunting

The problem with many budget rifle scopes is that they distract from disappointing glass with whiz-bang features like tactical turrets and add-ons like cheap rings, power-changing levers, and illuminated reticles.

​The Burris Fullfield 3-12×42 has none of those. Instead, it’s a throwback, built on a 1-inch tube with capped turrets and a second-plane duplex reticle. This is the scope that appeals to your buddy who wants to hand-crank their pickup windows. By keeping things simple, Burris has produced a new classic that might be the perfect deer-hunting scope in our test of nearly 25 hunting scopes. That it’s able to sell the Fullfield 3-12×42 for under $300 made it the unanimous pick for the Great Buy award in this year’s rifle scope test.

​The Burris had plenty of competition for the honor. Vortex’s 3-9×40 Crossfire HD has many of the same features, second-plane reticle, and fuss-free performance for a little less money. But we felt the build and tight handling of the Burris make it a longer-wearing optic, and we tested that hunch by subjecting the scope to our inaugural drop test, which it passed with flying colors.

​Don’t expect the Fullfield to engage steel targets way out there. Instead, this is a straight-ahead hunting scope. Think straight-wall carbine, slug gun, rimfires, or just about any deer rifle on the market.

​“It’s a set-it-and-forget-it scope,” notes tester Nate Ward. “Not a lot of moving parts to break or batteries to fail.”

​Indeed, the Burris doesn’t have an illuminated reticle, and its parallax correction is set at 100 yards. The standard plex reticle is intended to be fast but not precise, since there are no reticle holds in the image plane. Hunters who want more reticle references should consider Burris’s excellent Ballistic E3 reticle. If you’d rather have illumination, the Wind Ret reticle is available for another $100.

​The standard-issue Fullfield has some nice features, including distinctive red accents on the power-changing ring and turret dials and rezeroable turrets. But we also noted some misses. It has a distracting greenish coating that’s especially noticeable in low-light conditions. Its turret indexing is so tiny that it’s hard to confirm when you’re zeroed. And some testers struggled to get both the target and reticle sharp in the same focus plane beyond 500 yards.

But for a good image, simple and repeatable controls, and abundant versatility, the Burris Fullfield 3-12×42 checks nearly every box for a hunting scope. By doing it for under $300, it is the very definition of a Great Buy.

Nightforce is known for building battle-ready riflescopes for long-range precision shooting. But their new NX6 product line is designed specifically for hunters. I used the 3-18X50 F1 version with a MIL reticle on an elk hunt this fall and found it to be an excellent open-country hunting scope. It had strong image quality and low-light performance. It’s a hefty scope, but not absurdly so, like some other precision optics.

One of the key features of the NX6 line is the new FieldSet turret system. Once you’ve established your zero, any simple tool — a coin, knife, or flat rock — will loosen the exposed turret cap, allowing you to reset your zero and set the zero stop. The stop can be set a full revolution above zero, or 2 MILs.

One of the many cool things about this system is that any NX6 model except the 1-6x can be converted from capped to exposed turret, and the standard exposed turret can be traded for a custom BDC turret. It’s another indication that the NX6 is positioned to be the ultimate versatile scope family.

The scope comes with a versatile illumination system that lights up the entire reticle. This is a relatively advanced and expensive scope, but for spun-up riflemen who are looking to shoot deer at longer ranges, it’s an excellent option. — Alex Robinson

This short- to medium-range workhorse from Nightforce was years in development, but it was worth both the wait and the weight. While it’s a compact unit, measuring under 11 inches long and weighing just over a pound, the NX6 feels much more substantial.

That weight and durability will make this a battalion optic for uniformed services around the world. But it will also make it a very good pick for a 3-Gun competitor or a fly-in Alaskan bear hunter. Nightforce has had the entire NX6 line in incubation for years, as an answer to scopes like Leupold’s Mark 4HD and Mark 5HD, Vortex’s Razor HD and the Vudu from EOTECH. It was worth the wait.

We tested many configurations of the NX6 line in our other rifle scope tests, but the standout of the new family is this smart, sharp, and extremely versatile 1-6×24 LPVO. For bringing best-in-class controls, a smart first focal-plane reticle, useful illumination, and a built-to-last package, the Nightforce NX6 1-6×24 wins our Editor’s Choice award for the top LPVO in this year’s test.

The Nightforce comes in three reticle types, either the standard illuminated 4A duplex, the hash-style FC-6c BDC reticle that’s configured for multi-gun competition, or the illuminated FC-DMx in the first focal-plane, which is the version we tested.

The reticle features an illuminated segmented circle with a floating center dot that, on increasing the magnification, reveals a 1 MRAD aiming grid. At lower mags, the clustered circle-dot arrangement makes a coherent and fast red-dot sight. At higher mags, that grid comes into view and assists precision bullet placement out to as far a rifle with this type scope can shoot.

The old-fashioned locking eyepiece diopter is strong and reliable, but it’s also stiff and slow, especially if you’re trading the scope between shooters with different optical prescriptions. The eyebox can be stingy at higher magnifications. We’d like to see a couple of brighter steps in the illumination, and we think the sweet configuration for this scope is 1.5-9x so that the reticle’s precision references might have even more visibility.

But the Nightforce behaves as you’d expect it to, and its 6-times magnification range seems optimized for this LPVO platform. The controls are tight and smooth. The 30mm main tube is rigid and stiff. The entire unit feels like you could use it as a falling wedge in the big woods around Nightforce’s northern Idaho home. In our experience, it would probably excel at that task, too, and then stack bullets in just about any competition or hunting scenario you can imagine.

At $1,800, the 1-6×24 is pricey. But that price doesn’t feel out of line for an heirloom optic that will trade across not only rifle platforms, but generations.

Sig Sauer’s best-selling LPVO just got smaller, tighter, and brighter. The TANGO-MSR Compact brings all the versatility of the original in a package that measures a puny 8.4 inches and comes pre-mounted on a very good cantilever unimount for the screaming price of $399.

For packing in so much value in a tidy, powerful package, the TANGO-MSR Compact is our Great Buy as the best deal of this year’s Outdoor Life LPVO test.

We’ll detail the two things that gave us pause before gushing about all the features of this scope that make it a winner. The glass isn’t that good. We detected some pincushion aberrations that are noticeable when panning at lower magnifications, and the overall resolution is average. The eyebox is pretty stingy, meaning that when you throw the scope up to engage a target, it’s easy to be out of alignment with the image.

But everything else about this little marvel is spot-on. Generally, we like to see first focal-plane reticles in LPVOs because they boost the platform’s versatility. At their lower magnifications, FFP reticles act as a red-dot sight, and at higher magnifications, they perform as precision optics. But the second-plane arrangement in the TANGO-MSR — the MOA-based reticle is called the BDC6 — is nearly as useful for those purposes. The inverted-horseshoe center aiming arrangement blazes bright in daylight conditions, and the BDC grid is useful for placing bullets with precision on targets out to 500 yards. The only real tradeoff is that the scope must be set at its highest magnification for the bullet-drop subtensions to be accurate.

We put the scope through a battery of close-range fast-fire drills, and atop an AR carbine it’s a nimble and effective personal-defense scope. Then we slowed things down and rang steel out to a quarter-mile with the scope, using both its BDC references but just as importantly, its fine MOA-based windage dots to hold into the prairie breeze.

The TANGO-MSR is optimized for this AR-15 work, but it would be great on a straight-wall cartridge carbine, muzzleloader, or a pistol-caliber carbine, and it’s made for 3-Gun competitions. The super-compact size makes it a great fit for rimfires. And the price makes it accessible for just about any shooter. The addition of its mount means that it’s ready to rock, right out of the box.

Pulsar’s Thermion scope has been on the leading edge of thermal tech and performance since it introduced the XG50 in 2020. The platform has scaled up with each new iteration, and this year’s rangefinding XL60 hits new highs in sensitivity, run time, durability, and ease of operation.

The fact that a 1024-pixel thermal led a fairly small but impressive field of 1280-pixel scopes says a lot about the Pulsar’s ability to enhance image quality with a best-in-class display and processing that boosts contrast of its relatively underpowered sensor.

The Thermion2’s most noticeable upgrade is its big 60mm objective lens, but its 10-hour run time is impressive, and its 2,800-yard detection range is among the best in our test. As close readers of our test know, we quibble with the published detection ranges of thermals; we think “recognition range” is a much more useful metric. In the case of the Pulsar, we put the recognition range at about 550 yards, plenty for nearly any hunting situation we’d expect to encounter at night and among the best in our field.

The Thermion2 is built on a 30mm tube, and standard medium-height rings make mounting a cinch. Also easy: the scope’s intuitive 3-button navigation. One button zooms the image, another records or stops recording content, and the third navigates the menu, which is accessed via a rubberized button on the scope’s left turret. Zeroing is a cinch and field deployment is among the fastest and least confounding in the field.

“This scope fired up fast and was quick to deploy on the tripod,” notes tester Derrick Ratliff, who also praised the spring-activated lens cap that eagerly swings out of the way. The ambidextrous focus control, two finger-grabbing dials on either side of the rangefinder tower, is easy to operate, even with gloved fingers.

The round display is especially easy on the eyes, resembling the dimensions of a daylight scope, and the high-resolution display supports the sharpest picture-in-picture we’ve ever tested. Other plusses: the 10-hour run time and easy interchange with Pulsar’s excellent StreamVision2 mobile app. The rangefinder is fast and precise.

We handed down some demerits, as well. The frequent refresh is so abrupt and jarring that it interferes with operation. “I’m surprised the refresh is as harsh as it is given the price,” notes Ratliff. And we wish Pulsar would abandon its proprietary rechargeable batteries and join the industry movement toward interchangeable 18650 cells. The Pulsar cells are powerful, but if you lose one you’re on the hook for a pricey replacement.

But overall, the Thermion2 LRF XL60 is a first-order thermal scope. It’s fast, clear, easy to use, and was the consensus choice for the best weapon sight of this year’s thermal test.

If you’re looking for a do-it-all thermal, it’s hard to beat this versatile workhorse from DNT. The Hydra is probably at its best as a weapon-mounted scope, a role that is enhanced with its decent laser rangefinder and basic but capable ballistic calculator. But snap the DNT off its quick-detach rail mount, and the unit becomes a nimble thermal monocular.

​We tested this capability, zeroing the Hydra to our 22 Creedmoor, but then liberating it from the gun to scan the Texas brush country for pigs and coyotes. Once we had acquired a target, we clipped the device back on the rifle and made the kill. In the daylight, we measured this talent, timing the span between scan-and-fire and then assessing its ability to hold its zero. We could make the transition in under 10 seconds, with no appreciable stray in its aiming point.

​DNT claims the Hydra can also function as a clip-on thermal. We didn’t test this capability, but given its eye-filling display, low mounting profile that would easily mate with a low-power variable daylight scope, and generally responsive controls, we can’t quibble with that additional functionality.

​We liked the double-tough metallic housing and oversized eyepiece of the Hydra, and had no trouble zeroing or running the unit in the field. Its 1.5x base magnification is a little low, but it provides a satisfyingly wide field of view as both a monocular and a scope.

​The 4-hour run time was a little disappointing. We had to make sure to have charged 18650 cells ready to drop into the Hydra in the course of a long sit. And its display, optimized for pulling double duty as a viewer and a scope, appears to be far away down a long tube. The display has two features that are more distraction than aiming aids: a cant indicator that shows when the scope is off its vertical axis, and an angle measure that shows positive and negative incline. The image would be cleaner without those two adornments that don’t add much to its performance.

​But overall, testers considered the image to be crisper than its specs indicated, and the tactile LRF button is easy to find and operate in any of the Hydra’s three modes.

​“It’s a good option for a first thermal purchase,” notes tester Scott Einsmann. “It’s all you need for 100 yards and in. The mount needs work, though. It’s not particularly well thought-out.”

​Note that DNT makes 10 versions of the Hydra, four with laser rangefinders and six without, so be prepared to wade through a lot of options in the product line. But the HS635R is one of the rare bargains in the thermal category. For about $2,500 you get a serviceable viewer and a very good weapon-mounted scope with a solid build, an honest warranty, and plenty of performance. For all those reasons, the DNT Hydra HS635R is our Great Buy for this year’s Outdoor Life thermal test.

DNT Hydra HS635R Specs: Sensor Resolution 640×512

With this 12.5-inch gem, Vortex has redefined the form factor of a high-performing precision scope. While other brands have tried to package a first-order reticle and repeatable controls in a compact build, they haven’t been able to pull off the task as well as Vortex has, thanks to the index-matched ED glass from Japan.

The versatility of the latest iteration of the Razor HD elevated the Vortex just a smidge above its two other competitors for the best precision scope of the year, the new Nightforce NX6 5-30×56 and the surprising Sig BRAVO 6T-BDX 5-30×56 “digitally enhanced” scope.

Beyond the quality of its glass, which makes the Razor HD Gen III useful at both the lowest and highest end of its versatile magnification range, the Vortex’s controls deserve special mention. While the Outdoor Life test team found them a little tight out of the box, the turrets move with surgical precision and the pull-to-adjust illumination module is a fine piece of machining. The compact build doesn’t detract from dialing to your heart’s content. The MOA version of the scope that we tested has nearly 160 MOA (46 MILS in the MRAD version) of elevation adjustment.

The scope has a smart revolution indicator on the elevation turret. After you rotate a full revolution, a silver plunger protrudes from the dial. A second rotation futher extends the plunger, which has an O-ring to ensure moisture doesn’t work into the erector system. The system allows users to know where they are in the dial without extending the height of the low-profile elevation turret.

The EBR-70 reticle won’t particularly wow precision shooters who have come to expect its combination of speed and granularity. It’s fine even though we occasionally had to slow down to manually count windage MOA dots for some extreme hold-off shots.

For its ability to mount low on a wide variety of platforms, its dead-on precision, and its excellent glass and controls, the Vortex Razor HD Gen III is the Editor’s Choice winner as the top-scoring precision scope of the year. With a real-world street price of around $2,800, it’s a significant investment but for an all-around tactical, competition, and even hunting scope, it packs a ton of performance in its 12.5-inch build.

Outdoor Life’s Shooting Editor, John B. Snow, is a competitive shooter and expert in all things long range. He wrote an article and recorded a video on his top precision scope recommendations. If he ad to choose just one though, the Nightforce ATACR 7-35×56 is his top pick. Here’s what he has to say about this scope. Click here to read his full guide.

The Nightforce ATACR 7-35×56 FFP for a long time has set standard for this category. It’s durability under the worst battlefield conditions is the stuff of legend. No type of sporting optic is as complex (or subject to failure) as a rifle scope, and Nightforce built its reputation with products that could stand up to serious abuse. Beyond that, the controls on these scopes are superlative – the ATACR hits the ball out of the park with its ergonomics.

And the Mil-XT reticle is among the best out there. The zero stop is complex by today’s standards, but not difficult to set once you know how. In the not-too-distant future I suspect Nightforce will update the ATACR platform given its age, but it is still one of the most capable pieces of glass out there and one I turn to again and again when it counts, as when shooting ELR matches.

Like the new Nightforce NX6, we could write a tome on Zeiss’s new V3 family of second-plane scopes that are going to compete well with Leupold and Vortex for America’s favorite deer-hunting optic. We tested three versions with similar enough features that we’ll cover our general impressions before teasing apart some of the points of differentiation between the 3.5-10×42, 4.5-14×44, and 6-18×50.

​Note that this family is so new that we tested what Zeiss calls “pre-production” models of the V3. Some of our critiques, including indistinct turret clicks, have been improved in the mass-produced versions of the scopes.

The big news is that these premium Zeiss scopes are no longer made in Europe. They’re sourced in Japan, but if that suggests a decline in optical performance or brand integrity, relax. These represent the best of Japanese precision manufacturing, built around premium components and curated with American hunters in mind. That’s an important inflection; previous Zeiss rifle scopes were almost maddeningly European, with metric controls that often turned the wrong way.

The V3 line includes six models, from the rimfire-friendly 2.5-8×35 that will cost an appealing $300 to the all-around 3.5-10×42 up to the 6-18×50 that’s purpose-built for long shots in open country.

All three of our test samples featured Zeiss’s new exposed elevation turret with Ballistic Stop. The 3.5-10×42 has a dime-bright illuminated center aiming point but parallax fixed at 150 yards. The 4.5-14×44 has both independent parallax correction and illumination. Both these scopes have Zeiss’s Smart Hunting Reticle (SHR), which we found a bit too crowded. The 6-18×50 V3 has a non-illuminated XRR (eXtended Range) reticle, which we like better for fast target acquisition in dynamic hunting situations.

Like Vortex’s Crossfire HD family, the NX6 from Nightforce, and Leupold’s new VX-4HD family, the V3 has a number of variations on its basic theme of second-plane, 3-times zoom with prices that range from that $300 plinker to $950. Given the abundant attributes packed into the most feature-rich V3s, that price is right in line with its competitors.

The V3 has noticeably bright glass. Zeiss claims at least 90 percent light transmission through the entire optic, not just one or two lens elements. That brightness is achieved partly through wire-frame reticles that don’t require the additional lens elements of engraved reticles, but also with excellent glass and Zeiss’s proprietary coatings, which tame flaring, boost contrast, and maximize light transmission.

The test team appreciated the tactility and ease of adjusting the exposed elevation turret, but its operation held the entire line back from a higher score. The turret, with an impressive five revolutions of travel, wobbles slightly, and simply moves too easily. It’s important to note that turret performance is a function of the pre-production build. Following our test, Zeiss sent production models that have deeper detents and much more positive action in what could be called the “slow-speed” turret. The V3 dials allow only 10 MOA of travel per revolution, but because they have just 40 clicks, each gear is deeper and more positive than the shallower detents in “high-speed” turrets with 20 to 25 MOA of travel per revolution.

Because it doesn’t lock, some testers fretted that the exposed turret could get knocked off zero in a hard hunt. You can easily return the turret to its zero, thanks to the solid, mechanical ballistic stop, but we’d like to see a pull-to-turn locking feature on the exposed turret. Of course, you can always get the version with a capped elevation turret.

Our only other gripe was the crowded appearance of the SHR reticle. With its 1 MOA hashes clustered on both the horizontal and vertical stadia and no numeric references, we found ourselves counting aloud the holdover and holdoff references. We like the XRR reticle in the 6-18×50 better, largely because it’s more open, allowing for quicker, more assured holds.

​There’s plenty that we did like about this new V3 family. The center-dot illumination is sharp and bright, and enhances reticle visibility in the SHR configuration. The glass is excellent, with edge clarity and nice contrast, color fidelity, and that quantifiable brightness. We like the light weight of all the models. The 3.5-10×42 weighs less than a pound, even with the overlarge exposed elevation turret. We like the controls, which turn with style and confidence. Lastly, we really like the huge internal adjustment range of the V3. Some models feature twice the reticle adjustment of their peers.

​The entire V3 line is priced in the sweet spot considering its excellent glass, abundant features, quality of components, and impressive versatility of these light and very bright new scopes.

This might be the ultimate low-maintenance mountain scope. Zero this scope, cap the turrets, and go hunting. For those hunters and shooters distracted by the crazy amount of adjustability in a modern scope — exposed eager-to-turn turrets, busy reticles that require a math degree to comprehend, and illumination and parallax all requiring your attention before a shot — this stripped-down VX-4HD is your huckleberry.

​At 14.6 ounces, it is one of the best lightweight mountain-rifle scopes in this year’s test. “Belongs on my sheep rifle,” declared one tester.

​The team was sharply divided on the merits of this old-school optic. Half felt its simplicity was a feature. The other half thought its unilluminated “Hunt-Plex” reticle, 150-yard fixed parallax, and capped turrets are a liability in an era of scope adjustability.

​For the former, the 3-12×40’s excellent glass and “huntability” is the point. The fixed parallax didn’t affect focus; we were able to keep the reticle and target in sharp focus out beyond 500 yards, which is near the maximum range of this reticle. The eyebox is forgiving, meaning you don’t have to have a perfect eye alignment to see the entire image. Images were bright and vibrant in daylight, though the scope finished last in our low-light test, probably limited by the 40mm objective lens. The lightweight and low-profile mounting dimensions add to the Leupold’s versatility.

​But for the critics, versatility is limited by the unforgivable tactility of the turrets and the pedestrian aiming system.

​“The turrets are maddeningly hard to turn, too tight, and they have indistinct clicks,” noted one tester. “I can’t really hear or feel the clicks, and the turret indexing is very poor. This is a good set-and-forget hunting scope, but the turrets are a letdown, especially at the price” of about $800.

​The 3-12×40 version is the only VX-4HD with capped turrets. The rest of the family has the updated CDS-ZL2 elevation turrets. If Leupold revisits this model, it would further endear itself to those go-light hunters who want the combination of simplicity and a small measure of adjustability.

Like Nightforce, Zeiss, and Leupold, Vortex is completing the buildout of an entire rifle scope family. The Crossfire HD line, slowly replacing the Crossfire 2 line, has a scope for every hunter, from a handy LPVO to this high-mag optic that’s optimized for hunters but which has some stoke for target shooters.

​We tested other configurations of the family last year. This year we evaluated the 3-9×40 and 2-7×32 versions of the Crossfire HD line, so while this review is mainly focused on the 6-18×50 build, our perspectives apply to those other scopes with similar reticles and operating systems.

The 6-18×50 gained points for its hunter-centric BDC reticle, which has MOA-based hashes at 1.5, 4.5, and 7.5 MOA below the illuminated center aiming point. Those spacings conform to the drop of standard-velocity bullets zeroed at 100 yards or high-velocity and magnum calibers zeroed at 200 yards (Vortex ships a chart of zeroing recommendations with its scopes).

Users are encouraged to match their load ballistics with Vortex’s Long Range Ballistic Calculator to understand subtensions at various magnifications. That’s an important consideration, since published subtensions are only valid at the highest magnification of the second-plane reticle. For most hunters, who will throw away the reticle reference manual the minute they mount the scope, the 4-12×44 or 3-9×40 are more useful magnification ranges for the Dead-Hold BDC reticle than the 6-18×50 version. But when we plugged our specific ballistics into the Vortex calculator, we got magnification-adjusted holds out to 500 yards with center-fire ammo, and out to 145 yards with our 40-grain CCI Green Tag .22 Long Rifle load, which has become the go-to rimfire bullet for our test because of its consistency and affordability.

​It’s interesting to observe that the Crossfire HD scopes are only available in MOA configurations, and Vortex has leaned heavily into its Dead-Hold 2A BDC reticle. For shooters and hunters who want Vortex scopes with MIL references or first focal-plane systems, the Diamondback and Strike Eagle families have more options.

​The glass in the Crossfire HD line is underwhelming, with a milky veil and some edge distortion. The eyebox in the 6-18 is pretty stingy, and with no manual parallax correction, the focus on the 3-9×40 version is glitchy, with testers complaining that they could rarely keep both the reticle and the target in the same focal plane.

​Also of note: the 2-8×32 Crossfire HD was one of the few scopes to struggle in our drop test. After three drops from 36 inches on a pad, the scope’s zero shifted about 2 MOA at 50 yards. The 3-9×40 version passed the drop test with no detectable zero shift.

​Durability certainly matters, but we reckoned that hunters aren’t buying these scopes for the glass; they’re buying them because they represent a raging value for all-around hunting optics. Turrets tracked well. Controls are generally smooth and precise. And for scopes costing under $300, the Crossfire HD line earned mammoth price/value scores.

​“Easy, simple, hunting budget workhorse,” notes tester Todd Netto. “I think your average hunter would take this over the other $300 scopes in our test. It’s worth that price all day long.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8273. DNA Evidence Helps Convict Serial Poacher, Who Forfeited 2 Vehicles and Hunting Privileges for Life

Published Nov 6, 2026 4:25 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A Wyoming man is serving 96 days in jail after he was convicted and sentenced on eight charges of wildlife violations this fall in Fremont County, according to a recent statement from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.

Dakota Jordan of Lander, who was found guilty of poaching deer, elk, and moose since at least 2021, now owes the state $18,000 in restitution. He has also forfeited the animal parts, firearms, and two vehicles used in his poaching sprees — a truck and a Jeep. Finally, Jordan lost his hunting and trapping privileges for life, a penalty that applies in all 50 states.

“I do think the penalties are appropriate for his complete disregard for wildlife,” Jon Desonier, WGFD game warden and access coordinator tells Outdoor Life. “We take this stuff seriously. Guys aren’t just getting slapped on the wrist for serious wildlife crime.”

Desonier, who was named wildlife officer of the year in 2025, started investigating Jordan after a man came to his office with information about an illegally killed elk cow and calf in November 2024. Word of a poached moose and deer were already on Desonier’s radar, but the dots weren’t connecting. That changed during an aerial deer survey. A crew counting wildlife from the air spotted the headless carcass of an elk.

“We [had] spent a day walking around trying to find it and had no luck,” Desonier says. “We were not far, maybe 200 or 300 yards off, but they had a much better view from the air so it was easier to see.”

DNA from that kill site matched evidence found at Jordan’s property. Further DNA evidence proved damning: DNA from four other poached animals traced back to Jordan, thanks to a DNA database at the state-maintained forensics lab. Those hits included ivories from one elk, the leg bone of a second, meat from a third, and the European mount of a deer.

“I’m so thankful for our forensics lab in Laramie,” Desonier says. “They held on to DNA evidence and analyzed a ton of evidence for us. If it wasn’t for them, we would not have success in this case.”

Before the department could proceed with seizing the moose Jordan had poached, officials needed to determine if he’d killed it on state, federal, private, or reservation land. Using photos and GPS data from Jordan’s cellphone, investigators found the bones of a moose killed in 2022 and determined it had been poached on private land. The background of his photos included utility equipment, which was also key.

“We drove around looking for the transformer in the photo,” Desonier says. “A High Plains Power lineman saw the photo and sent us right to the kill site.”

Investigators suspect Jordan poached more animals than those in his conviction, but they focused on the cases with the strongest evidence

“In my opinion, this guy shouldn’t be hunting,” Desonier says. “He doesn’t have the mindset to respect wildlife. That’s how we got here.”

Read Next: Idaho Outfitter Gets Hunting Ban After Illegally Shooting a Trophy Bull in Utah

Jordan’s father also lost his hunting privileges as a result of the poaching investigation. He is banned from hunting for five years and also owes Wyoming $5,370. At least two additional suspects are currently under investigation in a multi-state operation.

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#8271. Best Hiking Socks: Gift Guide

Serious hikers and backpackers have many different socks for various conditions and footwear. You’ll be surprised by the variety, and they’ll be grateful to receive one or more as gifts. In addition to normal socks and dry-weather socks, hikers need waterproof socks, sleeping socks, compression socks to recover from injuries, splinter-resistant socks for cabins…and the list goes on. An army marches on its feet, as the saying goes. Hiking socks are a gift that keeps on giving, and they make great stocking stuffers too! Santa approves.

Darn Tough Socks are the hands-down favorite among serious hikers because they’re so durable. If you do manage to get a hole in one or even wear it thin, the company will replace it for free! Just send it in, and they’ll send you a coupon to order a replacement. I’ve replaced many pairs myself. A hiking and backpacking favorite is the Micro Crew Cushion Sock, available in many colors in men’s and women’s sizes.

REI Darn Tough2. Smartwool Hike Crew SocksWhen new Hikers try Smartwool Hike Light Cushion Crew Socks, they often stick with them for life. That’s brand loyalty! Lightly cushioned, Hike Crew Socks (formerly called PhD Outdoor) are made with Smartwool Indestructawool with extended durability zones. The crew height also adds extra coverage on the trails. These socks are available in a gazillion colors and patterns, so browse away! Sizing is Unisex. REI Smartwool3. Injinji Liner Crew Toe SocksBanish blisters forever with these ingenious Injinji Liner Crew Toe Socks. Wear these light and breathable liner socks under thicker outer socks as a first line of defense against moisture and blisters, or wear them alone as your go-to socks for everyday adventures. Made with Coolmax, these synthetic socks wrap each toe individually, preventing the friction that causes blisters. REI Injinji4. Dachstein Boiled Wool SocksDachstein is the world’s foremost manufacturer of boiled wool clothing (including their famous boiled wool mittens, which also make a great holiday gift.) Boiled wool is very dense, warm, and effectively waterproof because it’s so thick and tightly woven. Made in Austria, these socks are worn for winter hiking, mountaineering, and sleeping in a winter sleeping bag. Amazon5. Brushtail Possum Down SocksBrushtail Possum Down Socks are made from New Zealand brushtail possum fur and New Zealand Merino lamb’s wool, and they’re very thick and warm! They are rugged enough for hiking on cold days and make excellent sleep socks. Brushtail possum hair is hollow, just like polar bear hair, which provides incredible warmth and water resistance. While typical wool socks may stay warm when wet, they take forever to dry. If you get these socks wet, the water shakes right out, and they dry quickly. New Zealand’s possums are unrelated to the opossums found in the United States. For extra warmth, pair these with Possumdown Mittens, which are great for hiking on cold mornings! Zpacks Garage Grown Gear6. KUIU Ultra Merino Over-the-Calf Wool SocksKUIU’s ULTRA Merino socks are designed for high-stress outdoor activity where additional technical support of the feet is required. The style and shape complement a wide range of footwear while adding protection to your feet. Highly breathable and moisture-wicking, this sock molds to your feet, reducing shear friction and maintaining optimal skin integrity. Made with Nuyarn wool, they are stronger than the average Merino wool on the market, yet they boast the same natural odor resistance and comfort. Additional yarn thickness in high-wear areas helps protect the feet with cushioning and adds longevity to the life of the sock. Elastic fibers are knitted through the middle of the sock to maintain a strong grip around the arch and ankle, minimizing friction and blistering. KUIU7. Far Pointe Polartec Alpha Camp SocksPolartec Alpha fleece is an ultralight, gauzy polyester fabric originally developed for the military and widely adopted by the ultralight backpacking community for its incredible warmth-to-weight ratio. Highly breathable and fast-drying, it’s an efficient insulation layer that’s perfect for making camp socks to keep your feet warm in a sleeping bag or under a backpacking quilt. These Far Pointe Camp Socks are for backpackers and campers who suffer from cold feet at night, and at just 25 grams per pair, they’re an easy addition to a backpacking gear list. They’re only recommended for sleeping in or lounging around at home, tucked into your bunny slippers. Garage Grown Gear8. Western Mountaineering Flash Down BootiesThere is nothing better than slipping out of your hiking, mountaineering, or ski boots and into a pair of lightweight Western Mountaineering Men’s Flash Booties at the end of the day. These babies are packed with warm goose down insulation to help thaw out cold feet and give them some good ol’ TLC. The Flash Bootie is primarily intended for use indoors, in your tent, or even in your sleeping bag, but a reinforced sole does allow for quick trip to the head before bed. Backcountry.com Garage Grown Gear9. NRS 0.5 Hydroskin WetSocksNRS HydroSkin WetSocks are the ultimate liner for hiking through snow, streams, or other wet and cold conditions. They are thin enough to easily slip into your boots, trail runners, or sandals. The neoprene core insulates and protects your feet even when wet, and the 4-way-stretch PowerSpan outer layer adds mobility and durability. These socks are a must-have if you insist on wearing trail runners or light hikers when there’s snow on the ground. The added pairing snaps prevent you from hitting the river with only one sock. REI Zpacks10. Darn Tough Mountaineering SocksDarn Tough’s Over-the-Calf Mountaineering Socks are seriously warm. They have a streamlined performance fit (which means they won’t fall down) and are chock-full of merino wool for superior wicking and all-day warmth. Their over-the-calf height and extra cushioning make them ideal for long-distance hiking and climbing through subzero temperatures. Fine-gauge knitting ups the durability factor and offers a “put it on, forget it’s on” feel. Their fabric blend pulls moisture away from the skin and dries quickly for comfort. REI Darn Tough11. CEP Compression SocksThese CEP Compression Socks have many uses. They prevent blisters, significantly reduce swelling, and can accelerate healing by promoting blood flow for lower leg ailments like sprained ankles, plantar fasciitis, or Achilles tendonitis. CEP is the gold standard in sports medicine compression socks. You don’t need these socks very often, but when you get injured, which happens to all serious hikers sooner or later, they’re the key to healing faster. CEP Compression Socks12. Rab Vapor Barrier SocksWinter hikers and mountaineers wear vapor barrier socks in subzero conditions to prevent perspiration from making their socks and boots damp. Your feet sweat 1/2 cup of perspiration every day, and keeping your footwear dry is a significant challenge. These Rab Vapor Barrier Socks are worn next to your feet and then covered with warmer socks. Made from siliconized nylon, they’re completely waterproof, so no moisture can pass through. A curious thing happens to feet that are covered with a non-breathable material in cold conditions – they stop perspiring. It’s magic. Rab13. Sockwell Cadence Compression SocksWith graduated compression and minimal cushioning, Cadence compression socks offer Sockwell’s lightest-weight fit for comfort during prolonged sitting, standing, flying, or exercise. Crafted with fine merino wool and rayon from bamboo, with spandex throughout the socks for a superior fit and comfort, their moderate (15–20 mmHg) graduated compression promotes circulation, minimizes swelling, and reduces fatigue. REI14. WRIGHTSOCK Double Layer Silver Escape Crew SocksMade with patented double-layer construction, WRIGHTSOCK Double Layer Silver Escape socks deliver cushioning and odor resistance for many miles of cushioned comfort on the trail. Their patented double-layer, lightly cushioned design reduces friction, excessive moisture, and heat to minimize hot spots and blisters, while silver extruded into yarn offers natural antimicrobial protection, which inhibits the growth of odor-causing bacteria on the fabric. REI15. Darn Tough Steeley Boot Cushion SocksDelivering fully cushioned comfort from the toe boxes to the cuffs, the men’s Darn Tough Steely Boot Cushion socks are ready to protect your feet around the clock. Performance fit helps eliminate slipping, bunching, and blisters. Boot height sits mid-calf for added protection and warmth. #8270. This Public-Land Virginia Hunter Chased the Same Massive Buck for 4 Years

Published Nov 6, 2026 4:59 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Over many days of hunting a public mountain in Virginia this year Nick Dean had only seen three deer. But one of them was a giant whitetail buck he’d played cat-and-mouse with for multiple seasons.

“I had some trail camera photos of him, and on October 27 I had the buck at 40 yards, but it was too thick to shoot,” Dean tells Outdoor Life. “He was following a doe, and I just couldn’t slip an arrow through the cover to take him with my crossbow – so I passed the shot.”

Dean was understandably frustrated that he’d missed his chance at the buck he’d been after for four years. The public hunting area is steep, rocky, difficult to access, and there are not as many deer compared to other areas of Virginia.

“But in clubs I hunt I can only take one buck, and the challenge of taking a mountain buck is hard to resist,” says Dean, who works for an excavating company. “I like hunting the mountains and I’ve been doing it there for 20 years. While there are not as many deer as some other places in the state, there are some big bucks.”

Dean had another chance to take the giant buck a couple years ago during the muzzleloader season. But his black-powder rifle malfunctioned and misfired — again failing to capitalize on a close call with the buck.

But on Oct. 28, the afternoon after he saw the buck this year, Dean climbed 2.5 miles up the mountain once again to try for the whitetail. He decided to climb a tree at a different location on the trail where he’d seen the buck the prior day.

“It was about mid-afternoon when I got where I wanted to hunt, because I had to work that morning,” he says. “I found a couple trails about 100 yards from where I’d seen the buck the previous day, and I climbed up about 15 feet in a super thick area.”

Through his afternoon and evening hunt Dean heard squirrels chattering and scampering through leaves. He turned when he heard something behind him about 5:30 p.m. and when he looked he spotted the buck standing in a thick growth of mountain laurel.

“All I could see was his rack,” he says. “I pushed the safety off my Ravin crossbow, and when he heard that he looked right at me. He stared at me without moving for about a minute, but it seemed like hours.

“Then he put his head down, took a few steps into an opening. I raised my crossbow, put the scope crosshairs behind his shoulder, and pulled the trigger.”

The buck whirled and took off into a massive thicket of mountain laurel cover. Dean heard the deer plowing through the vegetation, then it became quiet.

“I wasn’t very confident, and when I climbed down with my stand I went to where he stood,” Dean says. “I found just a little blood, but no arrow. I called a few friends, and my dad, and a buddy who knew where I was hunting said he would be there as quickly as possible.”

His friend got there after dark, but with lights they found a slight blood trail leading into very thick cover.

“It was so thick we almost stepped on my deer,” Dean says. “The buck only went about 65 yards from where I’d shot it. But in the laurel cover you can’t see anything.”

His 100-grain Beast expandable two-blade broadhead had been plenty lethal, piercing both lungs and the buck’s heart.

“There was no dragging the deer anywhere in that laurel and steep rocky area,” Dean says. “We dressed and quartered the buck and packed him out like it was a Western hunt for elk.”

Dean estimates his 17-point buck weighed about 180 pounds, live weight. He will have the deer aged by a state official. But he believes it’s perhaps 7.5 years old, and the same one he’d been after for years in that specific mountain area.

“There aren’t that many deer in that region, and even fewer big bucks,” he says. “In my mind, it had to be the same buck I’d chased for four years.”

Read Next: A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Dean says when his taxidermist was caping the buck for mounting, he found a wound on its neck. Dean believes that confirms his belief the buck is the same deer he’d chased for so many seasons.

“Last year I was walking in to hunt and I jumped a doe, and behind it at 60 yards was the buck,” Dean says. “I shot at it as it faced me, and I was convinced I missed. But the slight flesh wound on the side of its neck found when it was caped, proves to me it was that same buck. My arrow must have grazed its neck.”

No official measurements of the buck have been made, but eventually Dean will have it scored by Buckmasters.

#8268. Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Be Afraid to Harvest Does During the Rut

Published Nov 7, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

If there’s anything deer hunters can agree on, it’s that we love to argue. There’s plenty to debate: scent control vs. hunting the wind, treestand vs. saddle hunting, compounds vs. crossbows — the list goes on. Unsurprisingly, the advisability of harvesting does during the rut is no different.

Like many hunters this season, I’ve been patiently waiting for any mature deer to slip up during the craziness of the rut. Because, alongside the lone Pennsylvania buck tag in my pocket, are plenty of doe tags. A couple days ago, after passing a few doe fawns and young bucks in hopes that a more mature doe or buck walked through, I began to wonder: How many hunters are purposefully passing does during the rut? And more importantly, is it a good idea to wait or shoot? That’s why I reached out to Lindsay Thomas Jr., chief communications officer of the National Deer Association, for advice.

There are two lines of reasoning on why hunters should or should not shoot does during the rut. The more does running around, one argument goes, the more bucks those does will attract. That camp passes does during the rut because a live doe might walk by and bring a big buck in on her trail, or to the area you’re hunting when she goes into estrus in a few days.

I fall into the other camp. I agree that nothing beats a real doe’s scent — which is why I want to put a doe down nearby. Thomas agrees.

“My personal belief is there’s no better attractant for bucks during the rut than a doe on the ground in your hunting area,” says Thomas. “There is no better attractant. I don’t care what’s in a bottle. I don’t care what calls you’re using, nothing beats it.”

Both Thomas and I have experienced just how successful dropping a doe near your stand during the rut can be. Last year I dropped a doe about 40 yards from my stand early into an afternoon rut hunt. About an hour later, two small bucks came in to check her out, both presenting broadside shots multiple times. I chose to pass those two, but had they been bigger, more mature bucks, one wouldn’t have been so lucky.

“Many other hunters I know have seen this strategy work,” says Thomas. “Dr. Grant Woods has got some great video that he captured showing a buck actually using its antlers trying to get the dead doe to stand back up. By understanding tending behavior, we know that when a buck separates an estrus doe from the other deer, she will typically bed down until she’s ready to breed. Oftentimes this involves the bedded doe laying for upwards of an hour or two just chewing her cud until she’s ready. So, a doe lying on the ground smelling like an estrus doe and looking like an estrus doe is not at all alarming to a buck this time of year. In fact, it’s totally natural.”

If you’re interested in trying to fill an antlerless tag and shoot a buck during the same hunt, it’s important to do your best to put that doe down close to your setup. It’s not unusual for deer to run up to 100 yards after the shot (particularly if you’re bowhunting). In my mind, if a doe piles up that far away, it lowers the likelihood that a buck comes into bow range if he cruises by to check her out.

True, it may not matter because a buck could follow her scent on the exact same trail she took and present the same great shot. It’s also just as likely that another buck cruising through the area catches a whiff of her where she fell and beelines straight to her. If she’s lying dead out of sight, you may never see him. Personally, I get down, tag her, and bring her closer to my setup as quickly and quietly as possible. (Plus, in Pennsylvania, you have to tag the first deer you harvested before filling any other tags.)

Thomas is less inclined to climb out of his stand.

“I don’t think you want to get down and spend an hour blood trailing if it’s not going to be an easy blood trail,” says Thomas. “Walking all around that area is a ‘no’ for me, but if you saw her go down in some brush and know right where she is and you can make it quick, dragging her into the open where she’s visual from more areas might be a good thing for the remainder of your hunt.”

It’s worth noting that it is a hunter’s duty to always ethically dispatch and recover the first animal you shot, so make sure to pick your shots wisely, make smart choices about the recovery, and, if you’re choosing to use the doe as an attractant, only do so on cold days where the meat won’t spoil while you sit for a few more hours.

Regardless of your opinions on rut tactics, the NDA has been a proponent of harvesting does as early in the season as possible to meet your properties management goals. Experts say shooting whitetail does during the rut can also support healthy deer herds. Since one adult doe eats 6 to 10 pounds of forage per day, managing the overall deer population becomes more crucial as winter approaches.

“There are three things that help produce good bucks: age, nutrition, and genetics. We can only control two of those, age and nutrition,” says Thomas. “And by taking a doe as early as possible, or even during the rut, you’re helping enhance nutrition. You’re bringing the overall deer density down [and] producing more forage for other deer to help get them through the winter.”

Read Next: Quit Worrying About Genetics: How Successful Deer Hunters Think About Antler Growth, Cull Bucks, and Passing Good Deer

In short, shooting does early in the season leaves more forage for the rest of the herd, enhancing the health of your overall herd, and enhancing the nutritional output of the habitat for your bucks, resulting in larger, healthier bucks next season. It’s also more difficult to fill doe tags the later you wait into the season as does get spookier and harder to pattern during the late season due to hunting pressure and food availability.

As we enter mid-November, many deer hunters across America are reaching the top of the bell curve of rut activity. In some areas, we may already be on the backside of peak rut. If you’re still holding your buck tag and a few doe tags, get out and hunt. If a big doe piques your interest the next time you’re hunting, you can rest assured that putting your tag on her during the rut is only helping your odds that a big buck might just come into your area to check her out.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8267. This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

Published Nov 7, 2026 1:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot. Every day or two it sends you a photo of a giant old buck, and now all you’ve got to do is wait for the right wind to sneak in there and hunt him. And then, all of a sudden, the camera goes dead.

It’s a new camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell? Welcome to the often frustrating world of modern trail camera use.

I’ve been field testing and running trail cameras year-round for several years now and in my experience, there is no camera brand out there that’s immune to malfunctions and failures. But my experience pales in comparison to that of Rich Howell of Trail Cam Pro. Howell has been objectively testing and experimenting with trail cameras for more than 20 years.

I recently interviewed Howell on the Outdoor Life podcast and he shared several reasons why hunters see so many camera failures in the field. Some of it has to do with how we’re using the cameras, and some of it has to do with how the cams are made (which is usually pretty cheaply). Plus, Howell hints at where he thinks the future of trail cameras is headed, and it’s all about making a system that is more affordable and useful to hunters. It’s a conversation worth listening to ahead of the heart of hunting season.

In the meantime, here’s why our cameras often go down in the field, and what we can do to fix them.

Standard alkaline batteries often don’t have the required power to keep a trail camera running reliably, Howell says. If you’re getting fine daytime pictures, but blank, black images at night, it’s a good sign you have a battery issue as there’s not enough power for the camera to fire the flash. This can happen even when the camera is displaying decent battery life.

More expensive lithium batteries can work well, but they too can have issues. Howell noticed that about 1 in 20 lithium batteries would go bad very quickly, (like within days of use) and sometimes this was enough to prevent the camera from working.

Howell now suggests that hunters use rechargeable lithium batteries, which have proven to be more reliable. Having a pool of these batteries on rotation will help solve many trail camera power troubles.

When hunters first jump into the cellular trail camera game, they often like to get their photos sent immediately. In the beginning it’s fun to get a notification and then have that instant gratification of seeing a deer photo.

But it’s usually more effective to have a cell camera batch send images every 12 hours or 24 hours. This is a key way to preserve battery life, and it’s also a more useful way to analyze trail camera data.

Personally, I like to have cameras send every 24 hours and then I review all the cameras everyday in the morning. Looking at all the cameras on the property at once helps me put together activity trends.

Howell says that solar panels definitely can help keep your camera powered, but they often have issues in the field. First, you want to make sure that they are facing south to capture as most sun as possible. This can be a challenge if you want your camera facing north. And second, squirrels have a tendency to chew through solar panel wires. If you’re setting up your camera and panel in the hardwoods, there’s a good chance a squirrel is going to get to it. In other words, solar panels can be a useful tool, but they’re not a silver bullet.

If you’re using the stock camera strap, you’re just asking for trouble. The tag ends of these straps always seem to come loose (triggering the camera) and you’re never able to position the camera perfectly on the tree with them. Plus, other hunters can easily spot the strap, which is an important consideration if you’re hunting public land. Howell suggests using an adjustable tree mount to make sure you can position the camera exactly where it needs to go. You can find a wealth of  trail camera information on the Trail Cam Pro website and by subscribing to their newsletter.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8265. Top 10 Resorts in the East for Terrain Variety (2027)

Terrain variety may not be the first thing you think of when planning a ski trip, but it matters, especially when your group includes different ability levels. A resort’s range of runs can make or break a group ski day. It can be the difference between beginners and intermediates riding lifts together or only meeting up at lunch.

Below are SKI readers’ 10 top-ranked resorts for terrain variety. Each has something for everyone, from hard-charging experts to those who still need help buckling their boots.

See the Full Rankings: Top 20 Resorts in the East for 2027

Score: 8.45 Other Strengths: Lodging, Nightlife Weaknesses: Parking, Value

“Great terrain, topnotch grooming, good services overall.”

“Families will find plenty to like if they have the budget for it, and adventure seekers will never run out of terrain to explore if they know where to look.”

“Great resort but even better town. Easy access from Burlington.”

Score: 8.46 Other Strengths: Lifts, Grooming Weaknesses: Local Flavor, Guest Service

“Slopeside lodging, waking up sipping that first cup of coffee and looking out over the trails.”

Score: 8.59 Other Strengths: Challenge, Value Weaknesses: Dining, Nightlife

“I like Cannon because it has a variety of slopes and a beautiful view of the surrounding mountains. I am a disabled skier, and I’m treated very well.”

Great variety, the snowmaking is on par with the competition, and the lift system, although dated, is pretty efficient in moving skiers up the mountain. Kudos to the new management that is finally addressing minor maintenance issues (like repainting the terminals on the Peabody Express and snowmaking pipe repairs) that have been ignored in recent years.”

Score: 9.08 Other Strengths: Value, Lodging Weaknesses: Lifts, Après

The green circles are isolated, so if you’re thinking it’s time to try a blue, you have to be ready because there’s no easy way down off Madonna or Sterling peaks.”
