Why settle for decorations that only last a few weeks? Create beautiful seasonal containers that can brighten your entrance well into winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Holiday porch pots are a cheerful way to decorate your home's entrance for the festive season. These outdoor winter arrangements look beautiful and welcoming when placed near front doors, steps, or entryways to greet guests during the holidays.

As October ends, the holiday season approaches. Families make Thanksgiving plans, starting a season that lasts right through the new year. This is the ideal time to start putting together natural holiday decorations that bring bright colors and greenery to your home's entrance.

If you are ready to jump into a creative gardening project for winter, we’ve got the ideas to get you started. The basic idea is to combine beautiful plants and greenery to make spectacular seasonal containers. But you should plan to have some fun while you are doing it.

The best plants for DIY holiday porch pots combine appealing structure with festive cut boughs. They should be hardy enough to survive cold weather and add winter curb appeal.

Why not start with an evergreen that nobody else on your block is likely to display? This silver Korean fir cultivar is one of a kind: a curious, fascinating dwarf evergreen with twisted, curled silvery needles. The twisted needles of ‘Ice Breaker’ Korean fir (Abies koreana), available at Nature Hills, have frosted undersides, making it look as if it is perpetually snow-covered. These little beauties grow very slowly, getting to 2 feet tall after 10 years. They are hardy down to -20°F.

It’s easy to find evergreen foliage plants without red berries, but harder to find red berries without evergreen foliage. That’s exactly why winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata) in holiday porch pots is totally intriguing. You can order a best-selling Berry Poppins winterberry holly from Plant Addicts.

These native hollies – growing in eastern Canada through the southern United States – are pretty plants all year long, but they become stunningly beautiful at the dreariest time of the year. They lose their leaves in autumn, leaving only the amazing crop of bright berries to light up your winter pots. They are hardy down to USDA zone 3.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Ornamental cabbages and kales (Brassica oleracea) are cold-hardy foliage plants that provide exceptionally vivid white, pink, red, and purple winter colors for holiday pots. They are technically edible but are not grown for eating. Rather, they are cultivated for their bright, rose-like center rosettes.

Ornamental cabbage and kale plants maintain their bright structure and color well into freezing winter months. For a festive container, they can be combined with winter-hardy pansies, berried twigs, chrysanthemums, or ornamental grasses.

Pick up a four-pack of Song Bird Red Ornamental Kale Plants from Burpee.

You may know these stunning plants as hellebores (Helleborus niger), or as Christmas roses. Whatever you call them, they make fantastic additions to holiday porch pots, with their shining white flowers and strong, dark green leaves. The only issue with hellebores is that they usually don’t bloom until January – past the heart of the holiday porch pot season. But some cultivars bloom just in time for the holidays, such as ‘Christmas Carol Early’, 'Jacob', and 'Snowbells', available at Plant Delights Nursery. The Christmas rose is usually hardy to USDA zone 3.

This dense, naturally round shrub is a perfect little ball of soft green needles. Its small size and low-maintenance nature make Little Gem Norway spruce (Picea abies 'Little Gem') a popular addition to your holiday porch pot. You can order a plant from Magic Valley Gardens at Walmart.

Norway spruce grows slowly, adding only about an inch or two in size every year and topping out at about 3 feet tall and wide. Don’t worry about winter weather – ‘Little Gem’ is hardy down to -40°F. The new growth emerges soft and bright lime, but by Christmas it will be a handsome forest green.

The flowers that give Heuchera its common name of coral bells only appear in spring and summer. By the time the holiday season rolls around, you’ll appreciate this plant's incredible foliage. Coral bells offer a wide range of leaf colors beyond green, including apricot, bronze, pewter, burgundy, and deep purple. The foliage often adds even more enchantment with scalloped, wavy, or veined edges. Select ‘Caramel’ or ‘Peachberry Ice’ cultivars, both available at Plant Addicts, for foliage with rich tones and holiday warmth.

Many trailing “spiller” plants work well in holiday plant pots, but few are better than the classic evergreen trailing English ivy (Hedera helix), available in an ivy variety pack from Plant Addicts. This hardy vine softens the edges of holiday planters and offers all-weather resilience. It stays vibrant throughout the season and works well with flowers or small evergreen shrubs to create a festive feel. The cascading leaves create a rich, full look, balancing upright or mounding holiday plants.

If you’re ready to create gorgeous holiday plant pots of your own, a few practical tips will help. Let’s get down to the basics of how to put it all together.

The base of it all is the pots or containers you select. Choose pots in materials that can handle winter temperatures, like metal, wood, or even plastic. Avoid materials that will crack when the temperatures drop. Get pots that are big enough, but not too big. Generally, front door holiday plant pots should be between 12 and 30 inches in diameter and between 12 and 18 inches deep.

You’ll want to use potting soil in the containers. Leftover summer potting soil works just fine, but it’s best to buy fresh, like Miracle-Gro Organic Outdoor Potting Mix, from Amazon.

Next, you’ll want to put in the plants, and I suggest using a classic thriller, filler, spiller design. Start with the thrillers. These are the tall, eye-catching focal plants that make guests admire the pots. You can use one of the taller plants you have selected – like winterberry holly or ‘Ice Breaker’ fir – or you can use cut boughs after trimming the stems.

Get ready to layer in the fillers. This is the place for medium-height evergreens or foliage plants. Coral bells or ornamental cabbage work well in this role. Alternate textures and shades.

Last, add the spillers, plants with draping or trailing foliage. These go around the bottom edge of the container so that they cascade gracefully over the edges of the container.

Creating your plant pots is fun, but you’ll also have to put in a little effort to keep them going strong through the season.

This starts with care immediately after you set out the pots. Give each of them a deep watering, enough to saturate the entire soil. Excess water should run out of the drainage holes in the bottom of the pot. Make sure that’s the case, or your plants will die of root rot. It helps to add pot feet to elevate the containers off freezing patios.

Don’t worry too much about freezing weather. It is normal for the moisture in the patio pots to freeze. Keep checking the soil and add more water if the top inches are dry. Mist the evergreen branches during dry winter days to rehydrate the foliage. As the weather cools, cluster the containers close to the house wall to shield them from winter winds and create a microclimate.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8163. The 15 Best Gifts for Birders and Bird Lovers in 2026

(Photo: Courtesy Amazon, Bird Collective, Uncommon Goods, REI, Bushnell, The Folio Society, Theodore, Moment)

Shopping for the best gifts for birders? Well, you’ve come to the right perch. Whether the bird lover on your list is happiest in the woods with a pair of binoculars, keeping tabs on the birds at their kitchen window, or planning their next big birding vacation, there’s plenty of bird watching gear and gear-adjacent goodies to fuel their obsession. We rounded up gifts for every kind of bird enthusiast, from useful field essentials and clever gadgets to books, games, and home goods that let them feather their nest (literally). So whether you’re shopping for Christmas, a birthday, or just because, there’s something here for every bird watcher in your life.

Don’t let a little precipitation derail a day in the field, and give them this waterproof hat. Its breathable construction helps prevent overheating during active hikes, while the brim keeps rain off the face and out of the eyes—particularly useful when trying to keep binoculars focused on a moving target. Even better, it’s packable, so they can bring it with them on vacations and not worry about it getting crushed in transit.

Birding doesn’t always happen in sunny, shorts-friendly weather. Kuhl’s durable lined pants add a little extra warmth for chilly mornings spent scanning the treetops without making them feel like they’re wearing a sleeping bag. Best of all, they don’t scream “birding pants” and are still cute and comfy enough to become an everyday wardrobe staple.

A smartphone’s built-in zoom can only do so much when a hawk or an eagle is perched high in the canopy. This 10x telephoto lens adds serious reach to a phone camera, helping birders capture more detailed photos of distant subjects without carrying a dedicated telephoto lens. When paired with the stick-on lens mount, they can simply twist on their lens and snap away.

For birders who want to document their sightings without investing in a bulky DSLR setup, this cool point-and-shoot camera offers an easy way to snap away in the field. It can be used on its own or connected to Nocs’ binos to bring distant subjects closer, allowing them to capture magnified photos and videos of their feathered friends. Plus, its tough, weather-sealed design makes it a practical companion for other outdoor excursions, like hikes, ski days, paddles, and more.

It wouldn’t be a birding gift guide without a high-quality pair of birding binoculars. Bushnell’s 10x50s bring distant birds into closer view, while their large 50mm lenses gather plenty of light for brighter, clearer images, even in low-light conditions. They’re also waterproof and fog-resistant, so rain or a sudden temperature swing won’t cut a birding trip short.

Give them a front-row seat to the backyard action—even when they’re nowhere near the window. This smart bird feeder uses a built-in camera and AI-powered species recognition to capture visiting birds and send photos and videos straight to their phone. It’s basically a wildlife documentary starring their own backyard regulars.

A birdhouse that doesn’t look like it came from the clearance aisle at Home Depot. Handcrafted in Portugal, the Koti’s sculptural design offers a chic nesting spot for backyard birds while doubling as an architectural accent for the garden. And despite its minimalist look, it’s filled with thoughtful details—a textured interior allows new chicks to climb out safely, while the 1.75-inch hole is the perfect size to let birds in and keep predators out.

Want to splurge on your favorite birder? If the $15M Kelly Clarkson bird is out of your price range, this clever piece of art-tech is the next best thing. It uses a microphone and bird-call identification software to detect nearby species, then gorgeously illustrates versions of its feathered visitors on a digital screen. Think of it as a constantly updating art print for their own backyard that changes every 24 hours—cool, right? And a whole lot more unique than another Audubon print or identification chart.

A little bird identification practice disguised as a rainy-day activity. This illustrated, 1,000-piece puzzle features a lineup of Eastern North American species, giving birders a chance to brush up on their knowledge while piecing together their favorite feathered faces. It’s also a fun way to get the whole family invested in birding—no early-morning alarm required.

Whether they’re just a fledgling birder or a lifelong bird nerd, a gift card to Cornell’s online Bird Lab will let them brush up on their avian knowledge. The self-paced online courses cover everything from birding basics and backyard identification to birdsong, migration, and species-specific studies. There are also classes on wildlife photography, nature journaling, and attracting birds to the garden, so they can learn a completely new skill that’ll take their passion to new flights heights.

You don’t have to be a birder to get hooked on this game (though it certainly helps). In Wingspan, players build wildlife preserves by attracting birds, collecting food, and laying eggs, with each species bringing its own abilities to the mix. It’s gorgeous, surprisingly strategic, and the kind of game that can turn a casual game night into a heated debate about everyone’s favorite bird.

Helen Macdonald’s celebrated memoir about training a goshawk to cope with the loss of her father is part nature writing, part personal reckoning, and entirely engrossing. This beautifully illustrated Folio Society edition gives the award-winning book a bespoke upgrade, making it a particularly good pick for the birder whose bookshelf is already full of field guides.

Keeping field notes when the forecast has other plans is… frustrating. This weather-resistant notebook is designed to hold up to rain, mud, humidity, and whatever else the weather throws their way, so birders can jot down sightings without their notes melting away. That way, they can record species, locations, behaviors, and other details worth remembering without a worry.

This classic diner-style ceramic mug from Bird Collective says it all. Even better, Bird Collective donates a portion of its profits to bird conservation groups, so this cup does some good beyond just keeping their coffee warm. And if coffee isn’t their thing, the brand has plenty of other birdy-themed gifts worth wrapping up for the holidays, including species-specific apparel, home gifts, and gear.

This crafty embroidery kit gives them a cute, tangible way to bring their feathered friends everywhere they go. It comes with a cotton pouch, 16 colors of thread, and a pigeon-shaped thread holder to organize their spools while they stitch owls, songbirds, and more. The finished product is handy for corralling field notes, pencils, or all the tiny bits of gear that otherwise disappear into a backpack.

#8162. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

#8160. Is an AI Data Center Coming for Your Favorite Trail? Check This Map and See

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

#8158. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the villages of Shimsal and Khyber jointly installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

If you’re planting bulbs in your garden this fall, try this simple but super-effective hack to stop squirrels digging up tasty tulips and ruining the spring show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freshly planted spring-flowering bulbs provide an easy feast for hungry garden critters as temperatures drop, and are often eaten before they even get a chance to grow roots. Tulip bulbs are always the first to be sniffed out as they taste sweet and provide the perfect high-calorie meal for chipmunks as well as squirrels. Crocus bulbs, too, are carb-rich favorites on the garden menu in fall.

If you’ve experienced squirrels digging up tulip bulbs, you’ll know what determined diggers they are. Gardeners are just as dogged, however, and popular tricks to protect spring-flowering bulbs include laying steel mesh or chicken wire over the top, disguising the appealing scent of tulip and crocus bulbs by planting unappetising allium bulbs alongside, and using bulb baskets. But there’s a far easier, cheaper and more effective way to stop squirrels eating bulbs, and it helps the bulbs grow well, too.

What’s more, this robust solution protects bulbs from rodents and other underground burrowers like voles, who also love to seek out this nutrient-dense food source in fall.

When you're planting bulbs in fall, the magic ingredient to keep these energy balls safe from squirrels is poultry grit made from crushed oyster shells. The sharp, jagged edges of crushed oyster shells means it's painful for paws to dig through, so it provides an effective barrier that stops critters eating tulip bulbs and even tempting crocus.

What's more, as well as keeping bulbs safe from sharp teeth this natural material improves soil drainage, making bulbs less likely to rot through wet winter weather. Crushed oyster shells also break down very slowly to provide plants with a steady supply of calcium, which supports strong root and stem growth.

Not all chicken grit is created equal when it comes to protecting fall-planted bulbs, however. Make sure you buy chicken grit like Pacific Pearl Oyster Shell Calcium Supplement for Chickens, available from Walmart, that's made purely from oyster shells as many products are cut with cheaper materials like limestone. Choose crushed shells (sometimes sold as chick grit) over flaked shells as this is both sharper on paws and easier for plant roots and shoots to grow through.

When planting bulbs in pots, simply add an inch-thick layer of chicken grit to the soil surface to deter squirrels from digging, where it will also act as a mulch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Opt for a double layer of poultry grit when planting bulbs in the ground. Add an inch-thick layer of crushed oyster shells to the bottom of the planting hole, and sit the bulbs right on top. This helps to protects bulbs from burrowing pests who typically attack from below, when a landslide of sharp oyster shells will send them scurrying away in search of more easily accessible food. If voles, field mice and pocket gophers are a particular problem in your garden, you can also pack a shallow layer of grit all around the bulb to fully encase it.

Fill the planting trench with soil as normal but add a second inch-thick layer of oyster shell grit an inch or two below the surface. When squirrels or other critters hit this sharp, gravelly layer, they’ll give up digging. This top layer can also help deter raccoons and skunks who don’t eat bulbs but are attracted to freshly-dug soil to look for insects and grubs.

Crushed oyster shells will naturally improve soil drainage and create beneficial pockets of air, loosening up heavy soil. The shells also release calcium as they break down, which plants need to build cell walls.

Adding a heap of oyster shells to your soil can affect its pH levels long-term but this hard material breaks down so slowly, that’s not a problem unless you have soil that’s already very alkaline. While some bulbs like camassia (wild hyacinths) prefer acidic soil, more palatable tulip and crocus bulbs both tolerate mildly alkaline soil just fine. Testing your soil with simple pH test strips like these from Amazon will instantly give you an answer if you suspect your soil is highly alkaline.

There are so many striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November, and using this clever trick will keep them safe from hungry animals in fall. Whether you view squirrels as garden pests or like to welcome wildlife into your garden, crushed oyster shells are a natural solution to prevent them digging up freshly planted bulbs in fall. Poultry grit is as economical as it is effective, too, so you get to enjoy those beautiful blooms come spring without spending a fortune.

#8156. “These Aren’t Victimless Crimes.” Vandals Deface Ancient Petroglyphs Near Moab.

Vandals scratched graffiti above ancient animal petroglyphs at the Bear Panel along Highway 279 near Moab, Utah. (Photo: BLM Utah)

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) announced on November 6 that it was investigating vandalism at two ancient rock-art sites near Moab, Utah, where someone carved names into petroglyphs, leaving damage that may be impossible to remove.

The incidents occurred at the Bear Panel, a rock-art site along Highway 279 near the Colorado River, and another panel near Hell’s Revenge, a popular four-wheel-drive trail in the Sand Flats Recreation Area.

“These images are a physical expression of the past, their connection to their ancestors and to that landscape,” Chris Merritt, Utah’s state historic preservation officer, told Outside. “They will now forever be scarred by someone’s thoughtlessness, and that hurts the continuation of culture.”

The BLM has not publicly identified any suspects in the two latest incidents. An agency spokesperson told the Moab newspaper The Times-Independent that the agency planned to treat the graffiti in the days following its November 6 announcement, although some damage may be permanent.

Under the federal Archaeological Resources Protection Act, vandalizing protected archaeological sites can carry fines of up to $20,000 and two years in prison.

Photos show the name “Meru” scratched beside ancient carvings depicting a bear and a bighorn sheep at the Bear Panel. At the second site, near Hell’s Revenge, someone carved “Craig W” across several petroglyph figures.

Merritt said much of the artwork at the two sites dates back roughly 1,500 years and reflects Ancestral Puebloan and Fremont traditions, along with those of more recent Indigenous communities. The panels are part of a larger cultural landscape around Moab, where Indigenous peoples once lived, farmed, and traveled, he said.

Restoring the damaged petroglyphs presents different challenges at each site, Merritt said.

At the site near Hell’s Revenge, vandals scratched graffiti directly across ancient carvings. Merritt noted that typical fixes, such as scrubbing the stone or trying to conceal the marks with pigments, risk damaging the original artwork underneath.

The Bear Panel presents a different problem. A crack in the sandstone just below the graffiti means that scraping the rock could create openings for rainwater, weakening the structure through freeze-thaw cycles.

“Five minutes of damage could take weeks of repair to do carefully to preserve the subsurface imagery and the rock face,” Merritt said, emphasizing that any remediation must involve consultation with descendant tribal communities.

Merritt said rock-art vandalism has become more widespread in Utah in recent years, a problem he believes is partly connected to growing visitation on public lands.

“We’ve always had folks going back to the 19th century scraping their initials on the panels, but what we’re seeing within five or six years is a pretty significant increase in the scale and distribution, hitting archaeological panels that have never had graffiti before,” Merritt said.

The latest incidents follow another case in March 2026, when the Grand County Sheriff’s Office investigated graffiti carved into petroglyphs near Tusher Tunnel, along an off-highway vehicle route northwest of Moab.

To combat the problem, Merritt said Utah is using its Protect Our Past education campaign and a statewide network of volunteer site stewards who monitor archaeological sites. Signage and fencing can also help discourage vandalism, he said.

In November 2025, a Utah woman who vandalized petroglyphs on BLM land near Wire Pass was sentenced to 12 months of probation and ordered to pay $14,853 in fines and restitution, according to a U.S. Department of Justice news release. She was also prohibited from entering BLM land during her probation.

“These aren’t victimless crimes,” Merritt said. “We need to find ways to catch, prosecute, and convict these folks, so it sends a message to future visitors that this is not acceptable in Utah or anywhere you visit heritage sites.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact Moab BLM Law Enforcement at 435-259-2131.

#8154. The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

Heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson)

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

As someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

If you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, New Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

The “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

Norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

Little leaves on an orchid's old flower spike may signal trouble – but a keiki doesn’t always mean the plant is struggling. Here's how to tell the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It usually gets spotted by accident, halfway through watering. The flower spike that finished months ago has a few green leaves sticking out partway up, and maybe a stubby root or two hanging under them. That's an orchid keiki. For a minute, finding one feels like getting a second orchid for nothing.

Then the doubt sets in. Read up on what a keiki is, and you'll soon come across the idea that orchids are more likely to sprout them when they're stressed or failing. Anyone whose plant has also dropped a leaf or two lately will find that hard to shake.

Stress can play a part, though it's far from the only thing. Heat, fertilizer, and genetics all factor in, and plenty of keikis grow on plants with nothing wrong at all. A few minutes at the sink with the parent plant will tell you more than the keiki does itself.

The name is Hawaiian – keiki (KAY-kee) means baby. Look closely at a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) spike, and you'll see small bumps along it, each wrapped in a papery sheath. Those are nodes, each holding a dormant bud, and once in a while one of those buds grows leaves. What grows is a miniature copy of the parent.

Keikis aren't an orchid disease or a parasite, and they can't spread to your other plants. They're simply one way orchids reproduce without seed. Where it grows matters more. A spike keiki sits up on the flower stem. A basal keiki comes up at the bottom, squeezed in next to the lower leaves, and on a moth orchid, that second kind can point to trouble at the crown.

A stem keiki growing on a Phalaenopsis orchid stem

Sometimes a keiki does show up because the parent is in trouble. Moth orchids grow from one point only, right in the middle of the leaves. Lose that tip to rot, or a break, and no new leaves can form up there. With energy in reserve, the plant may instead push out a basal keiki below the damaged tissue. Dendrobium canes that lose their roots, or their link to the rest of the plant through rot or injury, sometimes sprout keikis as well.

Plenty of keikis turn up on orchids with nothing wrong, though. On moth orchids, they come naturally from the middle and upper nodes of the spike, and certain species and hybrids are just more prone to it. Hormones are what flip a dormant bud into a keiki. Dab cytokinin, one of those growth hormones, on a node and it can pull a keiki out of a perfectly healthy plant. Crazy Keiki Cloning Paste, available on Amazon, is a well-rated product that contains cytokinin.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Long spells of heat as a spike finishes, heavy nitrogen feeding late in the season, and too little light or humidity have also been tied to keikis.

Some longtime growers take a keiki as a sign orchid care could use adjusting – a dim corner or heavy feeding is a good place to start. On a plant with firm, flat leaves and plump roots, a spike keiki usually isn't hiding anything. A basal keiki pushing up beside a soft, dark center is the one to worry about.

A basal orchid keiki growing on plant with some shriveled old roots

Start by checking for orchid leaf problems. Healthy moth orchid leaves are thick and firm, almost leathery. An occasional yellow bottom leaf is normal – the oldest leaves dry up as the plant ages. Several leaves yellowing at once is another matter, and so are newer leaves that have gone limp and wrinkled. Leaves that shrivel like that usually aren't getting enough water. And in fall, don't be fooled by a cold windowsill – nights below 60°F (16°C) can yellow lower leaves on their own.

Next, slide the pot off and check the orchid roots. Good ones feel firm and plump. They look green right after watering and silvery once they dry. Rotted ones are brown and mushy, and if you pinch one, the outer layer may slip off, leaving nothing but a thin string.

Now peer into the middle where new leaves come from. That's the crown. It should be firm and green. If it has gone soft, black, or wet-looking, crown rot has likely set in, often from water molds such as Pythium ultimum and Phytophthora cactorum, and rot that spreads through the crown can kill the whole plant.

One yellow leaf proves very little. Slow decline is different. If the leaves feel a little softer each time you check and nothing about the care has changed, look underground – usually at the roots, or at old bark mix that's broken down into soggy muck. Good news shows up in the same places. New leaves unfolding from the crown, or fresh green root tips near the base, mean the plant is still growing.

A basal orchid keiki has been left to grow into an established offshoot on this neglected plant

Did everything look fine? Then leave the plant alone, keiki and all. If the check turned something up, fix that and only that. Cut rotted roots back to firm tissue with something small and sharp, and wipe the blades with rubbing alcohol between plants. Fiskars' micro-tip pruning snips are narrow enough to get in between roots.

For repotting, use a specialist orchid potting mix, like Better-Gro Phalaenopsis mix, available at Home Depot, which is a fir bark blend. Use a clear slotted orchid pot, like these Holanhing pots, so you can keep an eye on the roots.

After that, water orchids sparingly until new roots reach the fresh bark, and water in the morning so the leaves dry before dark. Tip out any water that pools in the crown. Moth orchids do well in bright, indirect light, just not pressed up against cold glass or sitting above a heating vent.

The keiki itself can stay put. Without roots of its own, a spike keiki draws water and nutrients through the parent's flower stem, and snipping it off does nothing for rotting roots or a damaged crown. Many growers leave a moth orchid keiki alone until it carries a couple of leaves and roots about 1–1.5 inches (2.5–4 cm) long. Smaller ones often struggle on their own. Once it reaches that size, separating and potting the keiki is a quick way to propagate your orchid.

It depends on the damage. A moth orchid that still has some plump roots and a firm crown can come back once its care is fixed, though you may wait a while for the first new leaf. Rot through the crown is a much tougher case. So is a pot where you find almost nothing but mush. Even then, a plant with enough energy stored up can sometimes send up a new plantlet from its base.

This is where a keiki helps. It grew from the parent's own tissue, so it carries the same genetics and can keep that orchid going if the parent doesn't make it. Leave it attached while the parent holds up.

What if a declining plant has a green flower spike but no keiki? Try using keiki cloning paste, mentioned above, to coax one out, though results vary.

So it’s not time to write that orchid off, just yet, because of one odd growth. Check the plant it's growing from. If the leaves are firm and the roots and crown look good, the keiki is no warning at all, just a free second orchid hitching a ride on the first. With a little TLC, you can get that orchid blooming beautifully in no time.

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

You don't need elaborate floral arrangements or expensive accessories to make a Thanksgiving table feel specia; all it takes is a handful of colorful leaves, a few little pumpkins and some carefully chosen garden finds . Now if you'll excuse me, I think I'll be heading out to the backyard with a basket before all those beautiful fall leaves disappear!

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Alpenglow Gear Alpenflow Fuel Transfer Valve

Hoping to buy a gift for an ultralight hiker? Here’s the hard truth: Whatever you purchase will be weighed, then quietly stuffed in a closet. I know, because after a decade of thru-hiking, I’ve almost completely wallpapered my small room with all the copies of Wild I’ve been given. Thank you, but please stop.

Apart from heavy gifts, the last thing an ultralight hiker needs is someone else choosing their big three. The little things, though? That’s where a good gift can surprise them. This year’s picks tackle ten small annoyances of life on trail, from a rigid bottle that actually works with a filter to a sun glove that doesn’t plaster to your hands.

Single-use bottles crease, crinkle, and need replacing, but my original ThruBottle survived 1,800 miles this summer with plenty of life left. My only gripe was that it was too stiff to squeeze water through a filter. I’ve upgraded to the new ThruBottle 1000, which has a softer body and sheds nearly an ounce, weighing 2.2 ounces for a full liter.

The zip-lock bag you’d rather no one ever rummaged through has a 0.14-ounce alternative: this cap turns a compatible 28 mm bottle into a portable bidet. I find that it works best with a squeezable bottle. Unlike TP, it never runs out halfway through a section.

I sleep cold, and when the temperature drops on the trail, my ears and neck are often the first places I want extra warmth. The Shag Hood, made from Polartec Alpha Direct, covers them for 1.16 ounces, so I can skip carrying another full layer. Bonus: It’s gorpcore enough to wear off trail too.

My old half-finger sun gloves always came off inside out, and getting them back on over sweaty hands was a nightmare. The éclipse gloves have a thumb hole and mitten-style opening, so they slide on and off. They weigh 0.35 ounces and give me UPF 50+ sun protection on the backs of my hands, where multiple rounds of sunscreen have never been enough.

A camera buried in your pack takes no photos. The three-ounce Capture Clip attaches to a shoulder strap or belt, so I can grab my camera when the light is just right, instead of getting stuck crouching over my pack, still fumbling for it when the light’s gone.

The long handle keeps your knuckles out of dinner at the bottom of a freeze-dried meal bag. The 0.8-ounce titanium spork would outlast my hiking career if I could stop losing it. I found four on my last thru-hike, so I’m clearly not the only one.

A half-empty fuel canister is too precious to toss but annoying to carry. I’ve envied hikers using heavier transfer valves, but couldn’t justify the weight until the Alpenflow dropped. It weighs 0.09 ounces and transfers leftover fuel between two standard EN417 canisters, including those from MSR, Jetboil, and Snow Peak.

Leukotape is my holy grail bandage. It stays on through sweat, mud, and sketchy river crossings, and I’ve accidentally left a strip on for weeks. It’s gotten harder for me to find it in stores lately, so a spare roll is a keeper. I wrap a generous amount around my trekking poles instead of carrying the full 3.9-ounce roll.

For 10,000 thru-hiking miles, my pillow was the head of my dirty air mattress propped up on a water bottle, which rolled out from under me all night. Don’t make my mistake. For 1.9 ounces, the regular size is the real deal, and it packs down to the size of a pool ball. Pricey for a pillow, but I sleep better.

This 0.11-ounce Dyneema pouch stops loose tent stakes from rattling around in your pack. You don’t think you need one until a rogue stake starts working its way through your bug netting. Not that I, a seasoned professional and expert patcher, know anything about that.

#8150. The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more new climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

“We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”

Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.
